ISPA Unit 5: IT Governance


                  
                  Source Material 
                  
                


Syllabus (Unit 5)



1. Concept of IT Governance
IT Governance is a subset of corporate governance. It ensures that IT supports business goals and maximizes value while minimizing risk.

Alignment: Ensuring IT strategy aligns with business strategy.
Value Delivery: Delivering value to the business.
Risk Management: Mitigating IT-related risks.
Resource Management: Optimizing IT resources (people, hardware, software).
Performance Measurement: Tracking project delivery and monitoring services.

2. Frameworks
COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies)
A framework for IT management and governance.

Focus: Aligning IT with business goals.
Principles:

Meeting Stakeholder Needs.
Covering the Enterprise End-to-End.
Applying a Single Integrated Framework.
Enabling a Holistic Approach.
Separating Governance from Management.



ISO/IEC 27001 & 27002
International standards for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS).

ISO 27001: The Requirements. Organizations get certified against this. It defines what you must do (PDCA Cycle: Plan-Do-Check-Act).
ISO 27002: The Code of Practice. It provides guidelines and best practices on how to implement the controls listed in 27001.

Key Domains: Access Control, Cryptography, Physical Security, Incident Management, Compliance.



3. Objectives & Dimensions

Strategic Alignment: IT and business moving in the same direction.
Value Delivery: IT delivering promised benefits.
Risk Management: Preserving the organization’s assets.
Resource Management: Optimizing infrastructure and knowledge.
Performance Measurement: Using scorecards (e.g., Balanced Scorecard) to track progress.

graph TD
    Gov[IT Governance]
    Gov --> Align[Strategic Alignment]
    Gov --> Value[Value Delivery]
    Gov --> Risk[Risk Management]
    Gov --> Resource[Resource Management]
    Gov --> Perf[Performance Measurement]


Enrichment: Fact Checks & Extra Info (2025 Trends)


                  
                  ESG & IT Governance 
                  
                

Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) criteria are increasingly influencing IT governance. Green IT (reducing carbon footprint) is now a key governance objective.




                  
                  COBIT 2019 
                  
                

The latest version is COBIT 2019, which updates COBIT 5 to be more flexible and customizable for different organizational needs.

ISPA Unit 6: Host & Network Security — Attack & Defense


                  
                  Source Material 
                  
                


Syllabus (Unit 6)



1. Malware (Malicious Software)

Virus: Attaches to a host file. Needs user action to spread (e.g., opening a file).
Worm: Self-replicating. Spreads automatically across networks without user intervention.
Trojan Horse: Disguises itself as legitimate software but contains malicious code.
Rootkit: Hides deep in the OS to maintain persistent access and hide other malware.
Stealth Virus: Uses techniques to hide from antivirus software (e.g., intercepting system calls).

2. Network Attacks

Host-Based: Attacks targeting a specific machine (e.g., Buffer Overflow, Privilege Escalation).
Network-Based: Attacks targeting the infrastructure (e.g., DoS/DDoS, ARP Spoofing, Sniffing).
Web-Based: Attacks targeting web apps (e.g., SQL Injection, XSS - Cross-Site Scripting).

3. Network Defense
Firewall
A barrier between a trusted and untrusted network.

Packet Filtering: Checks IP/Port against rules.
Stateful Inspection: Tracks the state of active connections.
Proxy: Acts as an intermediary.

IDS (Intrusion Detection System)
Monitors network traffic for suspicious activity.

NIDS: Network-based (sniffs traffic).
HIDS: Host-based (monitors logs/files on a single host).
Signature-based: Matches known attack patterns.
Anomaly-based: Detects deviations from normal behavior.

IPSec (Internet Protocol Security)
A suite of protocols to secure IP communications. Used in VPNs.

AH (Authentication Header): Integrity & Authentication.
ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload): Confidentiality (Encryption), Integrity, & Authentication.
Modes: Transport (End-to-End) and Tunnel (Gateway-to-Gateway).

IPv6 Security
IPv6 was designed with security in mind (IPSec is mandatory/native).

Features: Huge address space makes scanning harder (but not impossible). No NAT (End-to-End connectivity).

Cloud Computing Security

Shared Responsibility Model:

Provider: Security of the cloud (Hardware, Network).
Customer: Security in the cloud (Data, Identity, Apps).


Risks: Data breaches, Insecure APIs, Account hijacking.

graph TD
    Attacker --> Firewall
    Firewall -- Allowed --> DMZ[DMZ (Web Server)]
    Firewall -- Blocked --> Drop[Drop Packet]
    DMZ --> Internal[Internal Network]
    IDS[IDS Sensor] -.-> DMZ
    IDS -.-> Internal


Enrichment: Fact Checks & Extra Info (2025 Trends)


                  
                  Ransomware 2.0 
                  
                

Modern ransomware doesn’t just encrypt data; it exfiltrates it. Attackers threaten to release sensitive data if the ransom isn’t paid (Double Extortion).




                  
                  Zero Trust 
                  
                

“Never Trust, Always Verify.” A security model that requires strict identity verification for every person and device trying to access resources on a private network, regardless of whether they are sitting within or outside of the network perimeter.

ISPA Unit 7: Information System Security Auditing


                  
                  Source Material 
                  
                


Syllabus (Unit 7)



1. Auditing Concepts
An IS Audit is the formal examination of an organization’s IT infrastructure, policies, and operations.

Objective: To determine if information systems are safeguarding assets, maintaining data integrity, and operating effectively.
Types of Audits:

Internal: Performed by in-house staff.
External: Performed by independent third parties (e.g., Big 4 firms).
Compliance: Checking adherence to laws/regulations (GDPR, HIPAA).



2. Security Auditing Standards
Auditors follow standards to ensure consistency and quality.

ISACA (Information Systems Audit and Control Association): Publishes standards like ITAF (IT Assurance Framework).
ISO 19011: Guidelines for auditing management systems.
SSAE 18 (SOC 2): Standard for service organizations (Cloud providers).

3. Incident Handling & Forensics
(Overlaps with Digital Forensics)

Incident Handling: The process of detecting and responding to incidents (Preparation, Detection, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons Learned).
Forensics: Preserving, identifying, extracting, and documenting computer evidence for legal proceedings.

Key: Chain of Custody.



4. Blockchain Technology
A decentralized, distributed ledger technology.

Key Features:

Decentralization: No central authority.
Immutability: Once written, data cannot be changed (secured by hashing).
Transparency: All participants see the same ledger.


Security Use Cases:

Integrity: Verifying software updates or logs.
Identity: Self-sovereign identity management.
Smart Contracts: Automated, self-executing contracts.



graph LR
    Block1[Block1 (Genesis)] -->|Hash| Block2[Block 2]
    Block2 -->|Hash| Block3[Block 3]
    Block3 -->|Hash| Block4[Block 4]
    
    subgraph "Block Structure"
    Header[Header (Prev Hash, Timestamp, Nonce)]
    Data[Data (Transactions)]
    end


Enrichment: Fact Checks & Extra Info (2025 Trends)


                  
                  AI in Auditing 
                  
                

Auditors are increasingly using AI and Machine Learning to analyze 100% of transactions (instead of sampling) to detect anomalies and fraud more effectively.




                  
                  Blockchain Trilemma 
                  
                

The challenge of achieving Decentralization, Security, and Scalability simultaneously. Most blockchains struggle to maximize all three.

Information Systems (IS) Auditing Standards - Case Study
Abstract
This case study looks at how Information Systems (IS) auditing standards can ensure the security, efficiency, and regulatory compliance of a multinational corporation’s IT infrastructure. The study focuses on “TechGlobal,” a financial services organization.
Key Concepts

IS Auditing: Assessing controls in an organization’s IT infrastructure.
Standards: ISACA’s IS Audit and Assurance Standards, ISO/IEC 27001:2013, NIST Cybersecurity Framework.
Regulations: GDPR, SOX, PCI DSS.

Audit Process

Planning: Analyze IT environment, identify risks, create audit plan.
Fieldwork: Collect evidence (interviews, observation, testing controls).
Reporting: Outline results, control flaws, recommendations.
Follow-up: Oversee implementation of remedial actions.

Key Findings (TechGlobal)

Strengths: Strong encryption, effective network security, robust incident response.
Weaknesses: Weak access controls, outdated policies, low cybersecurity awareness.

References

ISACA: IS Audit Standards, COBIT Framework
ISO/IEC 27001
NIST Cybersecurity Framework

Information Security Policy and Audit (ISPA) Notes


                  
                  NOTE
                  
                

Source Information:

Unit 1 & 2: Generated based on standard Information Security curriculum topics (Security Policy, CIA Triad, Risk Management) as the specific source files were unreadable.
Unit 3: Generated from the detailed “Cybersecurity Domains” presentation provided in the course material.



Unit 1: Information Security Principles & Policies
Core Concepts

CIA Triad:

Confidentiality: Ensuring information is accessible only to those authorized to have access.
Integrity: Safeguarding the accuracy and completeness of information and processing methods.
Availability: Ensuring that authorized users have access to information and associated assets when required.


Non-repudiation: Assurance that the sender of information is provided with proof of delivery and the recipient is provided with proof of the sender’s identity, so neither can later deny having processed the information.

Security Policies

Definition: A high-level statement of management intent regarding the control and protection of information assets.
Types of Policies:

Enterprise Information Security Policy (EISP): Strategic direction, scope, and tone for all security efforts.
Issue-Specific Security Policy (ISSP): Addresses specific areas of technology (e.g., Email Policy, Internet Usage Policy).
System-Specific Security Policy (SysSP): Standards and procedures for configuring or maintaining systems (e.g., Firewall configuration guidelines).




Unit 2: Security Audit & Risk Management
Security Audit

Definition: A systematic evaluation of the security of a company’s information system by measuring it against a set of established criteria.
Types of Audits:

Internal Audit: Conducted by the organization’s own staff.
External Audit: Conducted by a third-party agency.


Audit Process: Planning → Fieldwork (Data Gathering) → Analysis → Reporting → Follow-up.

Risk Management

Risk Identification: Listing assets, threats, and vulnerabilities.
Risk Analysis:

Qualitative: Using scales (High, Medium, Low).
Quantitative: Using numerical values (ALE = SLE * ARO).


Risk Mitigation Strategies:

Avoid: Discontinue the activity causing the risk.
Transfer: Shift risk to a third party (e.g., Insurance).
Mitigate: Implement controls to reduce impact/likelihood.
Accept: Acknowledge the risk and monitor it.




Unit 3: Cybersecurity Domains
1. User / Accepted Usage / Access

User Access Management: Ensuring only authorized individuals use IT resources.
Authentication: Verifying identity (Passwords, MFA, Biometrics).
Authorization (RBAC): Granting access based on roles.
Account Management: Creation, modification, and deletion of accounts.
Accepted Usage Policy (AUP): Rules for appropriate behavior (e.g., no sharing passwords).

2. Data Access

Goal: Protect sensitive data from unauthorized disclosure, modification, or destruction.
Controls:

Encryption: At rest and in transit.
Data Classification: Public, Confidential, Secret.
DLP (Data Loss Prevention): Monitoring to block unauthorized transfers.
Least Privilege: Minimum access necessary for the task.


Access Methods:

Sequential Access: Reading data in order (slower).
Random Access: Retrieving data from anywhere on disk (faster).



3. Physical Access

Goal: Protect facilities and hardware.
Controls:

Access control systems (Badges, Biometrics).
Surveillance (CCTV, Guards).
Environmental controls (Fire suppression, HVAC).
Asset tracking.



4. Internet Access

Controls:

Firewalls: Filter traffic.
Proxy Servers: Intercept and monitor web traffic.
Content Filtering: Block risky sites.
VPN: Secure remote access.



5. Email Security

Threats: Phishing, Spam, Malware attachments.
Controls:

Spam filtering.
Email Encryption (S/MIME, TLS).
Authentication Protocols: SPF, DKIM, DMARC.



6. Digital Signatures

Purpose: Authenticate identity and ensure integrity.
Mechanism: Uses Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). Private key signs, Public key verifies.
Properties: Non-repudiation, Integrity, Authentication.

7. Software Development & Acquisition

SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle): Requirements → Design → Code → Test → Integration.
Secure Coding:

Coding Standards: Naming conventions, comment standards.
Static Analysis: Checking code without running it.
Dynamic Analysis: Testing code while running (performance, memory leaks, security vulnerabilities).


Acquisition: Vendor due diligence, SLAs, and technical reviews.

Other Domains

Governance: Strategic decision-making and policy implementation.
Threat Intelligence: Gathering data on potential attacks.
End-user Education: Training employees on security awareness.
Security Operations: Incident response, disaster recovery.
Career Development: Certifications and training.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-5/Notes/Mobile-Fore.content:
Mobile Forensics Chapter 1: Introduction & Architecture


                  
                  Source Material 
                  
                


Chapter 1.pptx



1. Introduction to Mobile Forensics
Mobile forensics involves retrieving digital evidence from mobile devices. Its importance has grown due to the ubiquity of mobile usage in crimes, supporting both law enforcement and corporate investigations.
2. Cellular Network Evolution

1G: Analog voice.
2G: Digital voice and text (SMS).
3G: Mobile internet.
4G: Broadband speeds.
5G: Gigabit speeds and massive connectivity.

3. Cellular Network Architecture
graph TD
    MS[Mobile Station] <--> BTS[Base Transceiver Station]
    BTS <--> BSC[Base Station Controller]
    BSC <--> MSC[Mobile Switching Center]
    MSC <--> HLR[Home Location Register]
    MSC <--> VLR[Visitor Location Register]
    MSC <--> PSTN[Public Switched Telephone Network]


BTS: Connects phones to the network (The Tower).
BSC: Manages radio resources for multiple BTS.
MSC: The core switching node for calls and routing.
HLR: Database of permanent subscriber info.
VLR: Database of temporary info for roaming users.

4. Mobile Device Hardware

SoC (System on Chip): CPU, GPU, Modem (e.g., Snapdragon, A-Series).
Baseband Processor: Manages radio functions.
Memory: RAM (Volatile) and Flash (Non-Volatile/NAND).

5. Mobile Operating Systems

Android: Open-source, Linux-based.
iOS: Proprietary, secure boot chain.
Legacy: BlackBerry OS, Windows Mobile.

6. SIM vs USIM

SIM: 2G/3G, limited storage.
USIM: 3G/4G/5G, enhanced security and encryption.
File Structure:

MF (Master File): Root.
DF (Dedicated File): Directory.
EF (Elementary File): Data (SMS, Contacts).





                  
                  Security 
                  
                

PIN (Personal Identification Number) and PUK (PIN Unlock Key) are the first line of defense for SIM cards.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-5/Notes/Mobile-Fore.title: MF_Chapter_2
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-5/Notes/Mobile-Fore.content:
Mobile Forensics Chapter 2: Mobile Forensic Process


                  
                  Source Material 
                  
                


Chapter 2.pptx



1. Challenges in Mobile Forensics

Diversity: Thousands of models and OS versions.
Encryption: FDE (Full Disk Encryption) and FBE (File Based Encryption) make data inaccessible without passcodes.
Volatility: RAM and network connections are lost on shutdown.
Anti-Forensics: Remote wipe, secure folders, and physical destruction.

2. The Forensic Process
graph LR
    A[Identification] --> B[Preservation]
    B --> C[Acquisition]
    C --> D[Analysis]
    D --> E[Reporting]


Identification: Recognize device and legal authority.
Preservation: Isolate from network (Faraday Bag) to prevent remote wipe.
Acquisition: Extract data (Logical, Physical).
Analysis: Parse and correlate data.
Reporting: Present findings.

3. Acquisition Methods



































MethodDescriptionProsConsManualScroll and take photos of screen.Simple, no tools needed.Not forensically sound, limited data.LogicalExtract via API/Backup (ADB, iTunes).Fast, safe.Misses deleted data & system files.File SystemExtract all files (requires root/jailbreak or agent).More data than logical.Changes device state.PhysicalBit-for-bit copy of flash memory.Recovers deleted data.Hard on modern encrypted devices.


                  
                  Chain of Custody 
                  
                

Always document who handled the device, when, and why. A broken chain of custody can render evidence inadmissible.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-5/Notes/Mobile-Fore.title: MF_Chapter_3
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-5/Notes/Mobile-Fore.content:
Mobile Forensics Chapter 3: Mobile OS and Evidence


                  
                  Source Material 
                  
                


Chapter 3.pptx



1. OS Architectures
Android

Kernel: Linux-based.
File System: ext4, f2fs.
Data Location: /data/data/<package_name>/ (SQLite DBs).
Security: App Sandboxing, Permissions.

iOS

Kernel: Darwin (Unix-like).
File System: APFS (Apple File System).
Security: Secure Enclave (Hardware keys), Sandboxing, Code Signing.

2. Key Artifacts
Communication

Contacts: contacts2.db (Android), AddressBook.sqlitedb (iOS).
SMS/MMS: mmssms.db (Android), sms.db (iOS).
Call Logs: calllog.db (Android), call_history.db (iOS).

Location

Sources: GPS logs, Wi-Fi history, Cell towers, EXIF data in photos.
Tools: Google Timeline, Apple Maps history.

System

Installed Apps: List of packages and install dates.
Usage Stats: Which apps were used and when.

3. Deleted File Recovery

Concept: Deleting a file removes the pointer, but data remains until overwritten.
Flash Memory Challenges:

Wear Leveling: Moves data around, complicating recovery.
TRIM/Garbage Collection: Proactively erases deleted blocks, making recovery impossible.


Carving: Searching raw data for file headers (signatures) to recover files without metadata.



                  
                  SQLite Forensics 
                  
                

Most mobile data is stored in SQLite databases. Deleted records often remain in “freelist” pages or WAL (Write Ahead Log) files until fully overwritten.

2. Open Source Tools

ExifTool: Extracts metadata from images.

3. Emerging Trends (2025)


                  
                  Future Challenges 
                  
                


Cloud Forensics: As storage moves to cloud, physical device extraction yields less.
IoT: Smartwatches and Home devices are the new witnesses.
App Encryption: Signal/Telegram encryption requires capturing keys from RAM or using specialized agents.

The forensic methodology applied to a device is fundamentally dictated by its operating system. The mobile landscape is a duopoly of Android and iOS, each presenting distinct architectural challenges.
5. Mobile Forensics Process
6. Forensic Tools and Technologies
7. Future Directions and Emerging Trends

1. Evolution and Theoretical Framework
1.1 Defining the Discipline
Mobile Forensics: The rigorous process of recovering digital evidence from a mobile device under forensically sound conditions, ensuring:

Preservation
Identification
Extraction
Documentation
Interpretation of digital data

Scope:

Internal device memory
SIM/USIM cards
External memory cards (SD/MMC)
Cloud-based backups

1.2 Unique Challenges

























ChallengeImpactHardware/OS FragmentationThousands of device models, customized Android versionsData VolatilityAlways-on, always-connected, continuous background processesSecurity & EncryptionSecure Enclave (iOS), TEE (Android), hardware-backed encryptionFlash MemoryGarbage Collection actively destroys deleted data


                  
                  WARNING
                  
                

Traditional “chip-off” extraction is ineffective on modern encrypted devices (Android 6.0+, iPhone 4S+) because keys remain in CPU/Secure Enclave.



2. Cellular Network Infrastructure
2.1 Generational Evolution















































GenerationTechnologyKey FeaturesForensic Relevance1GAnalog (AMPS, NMT)Basic voice, FDMAMinimal - no encryption, no data storage2GDigital (GSM, CDMA)SIM cards, SMS, A5/1 encryptionHigh - Established IMSI, SMS/call logs2.5G/2.75GPacket (GPRS, EDGE)Rudimentary internet, always-onModerate - Email, basic web artifacts3GBroadband (UMTS, HSPA)Video calling, 2Mbps+Significant - Smartphones, apps, multimedia4G (LTE)All-IP NetworkHD streaming, VolTE, cloud syncCritical - Cloud storage, voice as data5GHyper-ConnectivityMM-wave, IoT, GigabitEmerging - Edge cloud, IoT/vehicle telemetry
1G to 2G: The Digital Transformation

1G: Analog, FDMA, insecure
2G (GSM): Digital signaling, TDMA, introduced SIM (decoupled identity from hardware)
Created two forensic targets: SIM card (subscriber data) + Handset (hardware data)

3G to 4G: Smartphone Era

4G: Entirely packet-switched (IP-based)
Voice calls = data (VoLTE)
High bandwidth → apps, social media, cloud sync
Exponential increase in evidence volume/variety

2.2 GSM Network Architecture and Forensic Artifacts

The GSM network architecture remains the reference model for understanding cellular communications. It is composed of three primary subsystems, each generating specific data points valuable to investigators.
GSM Security Algorithms
sequenceDiagram
    participant Network
    participant SIM
    participant Device
    
    Note over Network,Device: Authentication Process
    
    Network->>SIM: RAND (128-bit random)
    
    Note over SIM: A3 Algorithm
    SIM->>SIM: A3(RAND, Ki) → SRES
    
    Note over SIM: A8 Algorithm
    SIM->>SIM: A8(RAND, Ki) → Kc
    
    SIM->>Network: SRES (32-bit response)
    
    Note over Network: Validates SRES match
    
    Network->>Device: Authentication Success
    
    Note over Device: A5 Algorithm (in hardware)
    Device->>Device: Use Kc to encrypt<br/>air interface traffic
    
    Note over Network,Device: 🔒 Secure Communication

The security of the GSM network relies on a triplet of algorithms stored on the SIM and in the network’s Authentication Center (AuC). These algorithms ensure that the sensitive Authentication Key (K_i) never leaves the SIM card.

Base Station Subsystem (BSS)

BTS (Base Transceiver Station): Physical tower defining the cell
BSC (Base Station Controller): Manages radio resources for multiple BTSs

Forensic Application: Cell Site Analysis - triangulate device location using BTS/sector data

3. Mobile Device Hardware Architecture
3.1 System on Chip (SoC)
Integration: CPU, GPU, Baseband Processor (modem), Secure Element on single silicon die
Examples: Qualcomm Snapdragon, Apple A-Series, Samsung Exynos
Baseband Processor:

Manages all radio functions (GSM/LTE/5G)
Runs separate RTOS distinct from main OS
Communicates with Application Processor via AT commands

BootROM Exploits:

First code executed on power-up
Hardware-level vulnerabilities (e.g., checkm8 on Apple A5-A11) are unpatchable
Allow forensic bypass of boot chains for physical image acquisition

3.2 Flash Memory Challenges
NAND Flash (eMMC or UFS):
Wear Leveling:

Distributes writes evenly to prolong lifespan
Logical address ≠ fixed physical address

Garbage Collection (GC) & TRIM:

File deletion → OS marks as invalid
Flash controller actively erases invalid blocks during idle
TRIM command accelerates sanitization
Impact: Deleted data can be destroyed within minutes



                  
                  IMPORTANT
                  
                

Speed is paramount in mobile acquisition - background GC process permanently destroys recoverable data.


3.3 Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) Forensics
SIM Structure (ISO 7816-4):

    B --> D["EF_IMSI<br/>6F07<br/>Subscriber Identity"]

GSM Security Algorithms


A3 (Authentication):

Network sends RAND (128-bit random)
SIM: A3(RAND, Ki) → SRES (32-bit response)
Network validates SRES match



A8 (Key Generation):

A8(RAND, Ki) → Kc (64-bit ciphering key)



A5 (Encryption):

Stream cipher in device hardware (not SIM)
Uses Kc to encrypt air interface traffic



Security: Ki never leaves SIM; interception doesn’t yield key. SIM cloning requires physical access + side-channel attacks on weak implementations (COMP128v1).

4. Mobile Operating Systems
4.1 Android Architecture
Built on: Modified Linux Kernel
Layer Structure

Linux Kernel: Process/memory management, hardware drivers, foundational security (UIDs)
HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer): Interface between software and hardware (camera, Bluetooth)
Android Runtime (ART): Executes app bytecode; AOT compilation (converts bytecode → native on install)
Application Framework: UI and resource management
System Apps: Core apps (Phone, Contacts, SMS)

File Systems & Partitions






























PartitionPurposeForensic Note/bootKernel and ramdiskBoot artifacts/systemOS files (read-only)Alterations indicate root compromise/dataPRIMARY TARGETInstalled apps, databases, user settings/cacheTemporary data, OTA logsApp installation fragments, browser cache
File Systems:

EXT4: Standard Linux journaling FS; journaling aids deleted file metadata recovery
F2FS (Flash-Friendly): Log-structured for NAND optimization; complicates carving (sequential writes, not in-place overwrites)

Android Security

App Sandboxing: Each app = unique UID; prevents inter-app data access
Full Disk Encryption (FDE) or File-Based Encryption (FBE):

FBE: Different files encrypted with different keys
Allows some functions before passcode (Direct Boot mode) while securing sensitive data



4.2 iOS Architecture
Built on: Darwin Kernel (Unix-like)
Layer Structure

Core OS: XNU kernel, low-level drivers
Core Services: Networking, Core Foundation, SQLite
Media Layer: Audio, video, graphics
Cocoa Touch: Touch-based UI framework

File Systems

HFS+: Legacy hierarchical file system
APFS (Apple File System): Introduced iOS 10.3

Optimized for Flash/SSD
Copy-on-Write (CoW): Edits written to new blocks → inherent data snapshots (forensic benefit)
Tight encryption integration: Data recovery without keys nearly impossible



iOS Security Model
Secure Boot Chain:

BootROM → Low Level Bootloader → iBoot → Kernel
Each step cryptographically signed by Apple
Signature fail → Recovery Mode (prevents custom forensic bootloaders)

Secure Enclave Processor (SEP):

Dedicated coprocessor for crypto operations
Stores device Unique ID (UID) fused in silicon
UID not accessible to OS or forensic tools
Prevents offline brute-force (passcode must be tested on device with hardware delays)

Data Protection Classes:

Complete Protection: Inaccessible until device unlocked
Protected Until First User Authentication: Accessible after first unlock

Device States:

BFU (Before First Unlock): Encryption keys not loaded
AFU (After First Unlock): Keys loaded in RAM - some logical extraction possible


5. Mobile Forensics Process
5.1 Phase 1: Identification and Preservation
Network Isolation:

Mobile devices are radios - can be remotely wiped
Incoming messages overwrite data
Solutions: Faraday bags or Airplane Mode (if won’t lock device)

Power Management:

Device ON: Keep ON and charged (maintain AFU state with decrypted keys in RAM)
Device OFF: Leave OFF to prevent boot authentication/data alteration

5.2 Phase 2: Data Acquisition Methodologies

Advanced Hardware Acquisition

When software methods fail (e.g., locked device, broken screen), hardware-level techniques are employed.
JTAG (Joint Test Action Group):

Solder wires to Test Access Ports on motherboard
Instruct processor to dump memory
Non-destructive but slow; requires partially functional device

ISP (In-System Programming):

Direct connection to flash chip (eMMC/UFS)
Bypass processor entirely
Faster than JTAG; requires precision soldering

Chip-Off:

Physically desolder memory chip (~240°C heat gun)
Read in specialized socket reader
Destroys device; only option for severe physical damage
Limitation: Ineffective on encrypted devices (key left in CPU/Secure Enclave)

5.3 Phase 3: Examination and Analysis
File Carving
Recover files from unallocated space via content signatures:

























File TypeHeaderFooterJPEG0xFF 0xD80xFF 0xD9PDF%PDF%%EOFZIP/OfficePK (0x50 0x4B)Variable
Tools: Scalpel, Foremost
SQLite Database Forensics
Majority of mobile data in SQLite (.db, .sqlite):

SMS, WhatsApp, Browser History, Contacts

Recovery Methods:

Active data: SQL queries
Deleted records:

Freelists within database
Write-Ahead Log (WAL) files (.db-wal) before overwrite



Key Artifact Locations
Android:

Contacts: /data/data/com.android.providers.contacts/databases/contacts2.db
SMS: /data/data/com.android.providers.telephony/databases/mmssms.db
WhatsApp: /data/data/com.whatsapp/databases/msgstore.db (often encrypted as msgstore.db.cryptXX)

iOS:

SMS/iMessage: /private/var/mobile/Library/SMS/sms.db
Call History: /private/var/wireless/Library/CallHistory/call_history.db


6. Forensic Tools and Technologies
6.1 Commercial Solutions

























ToolKey StrengthsTargetCellebrite UFEDIndustry standard; physical extraction; bootloader exploits (EDL mode); Physical Analyzer softwareLaw EnforcementOxygen Forensic DetectiveCloud forensics; 35,000+ device profiles; KeyScout for credentials; drone analysisEnterpriseMSAB XRYSecure .xry file format; strict chain of custody complianceEuropean Law Enforcement
6.2 Open Source Tools

Autopsy: Disk forensics platform with Android analysis modules (call logs, SMS, web)
ADB (Android Debug Bridge):

adb backup: Create logical backups (.ab)
adb pull: Retrieve specific files (requires USB debugging)


Volatility: Premier RAM forensics framework

6.3 Capability Comparison



































FeatureCellebrite UFEDOxygen Forensic DetectiveParaben iRecovery StickExtractionPhysical, File System, LogicalPhysical, File System, CloudLogical (Active + Deleted DB)Lock BypassAdvanced (EDL, bootloader exploits)Advanced (brute-force modules)Limited (usually requires passcode)StrengthBroadest device support, physical extractionCloud extraction, app parsing versatilitySimplicity, iOS specializationCostHigh (Enterprise)High (Enterprise)Low (Consumer)

7. Future Directions and Emerging Trends
7.1 The Encryption Barrier

Default encryption (FBE, Data Protection) pushing away from Chip-off/JTAG
Gray-Box Forensics: Utilize vendor-specific vulnerabilities (like checkm8) for privileged access without passcode

7.2 Cloud and IoT Forensics
Cloud Forensics:

Device becomes access token rather than sole evidence repository
Legal extraction from iCloud, Google Drive, social media
Use device “tokens” to authenticate to cloud without user password

IoT & Vehicle Forensics:

Vehicles generate massive telemetry (location, connections)
Infotainment systems forensically acquirable
Reconstruct accidents, track movements

7.3 AI and Automation
Challenge: 1TB smartphone data volume unmanageable for human review
Solutions:

AI/ML integration in forensic tools
Automatic image categorization (weapons, drugs)
Flag suspicious chat patterns
Correlate entities across terabytes


Key Exam Preparation Points


                  
                  IMPORTANT
                  
                

Master These Concepts:

SIM File Structure: MF → DF → EF hierarchy; key EFs (EF_SMS, EF_IMSI, EF_LOCI)
GSM Security: A3 (auth), A5 (encryption), A8 (key gen)
Cellular Generations: Evolution from 1G analog to 5G hyper-connectivity
Android vs iOS:

Android: Linux kernel, ext4/f2fs, app sandboxing, FDE/FBE
iOS: Darwin kernel, APFS, Secure Enclave, BFU/AFU states


Acquisition Methods: Logical vs File System vs Physical - pros/cons
Hardware Methods: JTAG (test ports), ISP (flash chip direct), Chip-off (desolder)
Artifact Locations: SQLite databases for SMS, contacts, WhatsApp
File Carving: Signature-based recovery (JPEG: FF D8 FF)
Flash Memory: Wear leveling, Garbage Collection, TRIM command impact
Future Trends: Cloud forensics, encryption challenges, AI automation




Critical Challenges Overview



































ChallengeDescriptionForensic ResponseEncryptionHardware-backed; default on modern devicesLive acquisition, cloud backups, exploitsFragmentationThousands of Android modelsDiversified toolkit; commercial toolsGarbage CollectionActive deletion in flash memorySpeed critical - acquire immediatelySecure EnclaveHardware crypto; UID in siliconLogical extraction, checkm8 exploit (A5-A11)Cloud MigrationData off-deviceCloud forensics, token extraction

Conclusion
Mobile forensics requires expertise spanning:

Investigative skills: Evidence procedures
Computer science: OS architectures, file systems
Electrical engineering: SoC, flash memory, hardware extraction

Core Principles (unchanging):

Preservation of evidence
Rigorous tool validation
Methodical reconstruction of digital events

Adaptation (essential):

New architectures (5G, IoT)
File systems (F2FS, APFS)
Security models (Secure Enclave, TEE)



                  
                  TIP
                  
                

The successful forensic investigator of the future adapts to technological change while maintaining scientific rigor.

Introduction to Mobile Forensics Mobile forensics involves retrieving digital evidence from mobile devices. Importance has grown due to mobile usage in crimes. Supports law enforcement and corporate investigations.
Index Cellular Network Evolution of Cellular Network & its History Cellular Network Architecture and Technologies Mobile Device Hardware Evolution of Mobile Devices & its History Mobile Device Architecture and Technologies Mobile Operating System Smart Cards Subscriber Identification Module (SIM/USIM) SIM/USIM File Management SIM/USIM Security


Cellular network Cellular network technology has evolved significantly, transitioning from basic voice communication to high-speed data and advanced applications. The evolution is marked by generations, each bringing new capabilities and features: 1G provided analog voice, 2G introduced digital and text, 3G enabled mobile internet, 4G offered broadband speeds, and 5G promises gigabit speeds and enhanced connectivity.


Evolution of Cellular Network


Cellular Network Architecture


Cont. BTS (Base Transceiver Station): Connects phones to network. MSC (Mobile Switching Center): Routing and call setup. HLR (Home Location Register): Stores subscriber data. VLR (Visitor Location Register): Temporary data during roaming. BSC (Base Station Controller): central management entity for multiple Base Transceiver Stations (BTS) used in 2G (GSM) RNC (Radio Network Controller): manage radio resources and facilitate communication between mobile devices used in 3G (UMTS) MGW (Media Gateway): bridge between different types of networks (like voice or video) in call PSDN (Public Switched Data Network) and ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network): are technologies that relate to data and voice transmission


M obile Device Hardware Components System on Chip (SoC): Integrates CPU, GPU, modem. RAM and Flash Memory: Temporary and permanent storage. Baseband Processor: Handles radio communication. Sensors: Accelerometer, GPS, etc. Power IC: Manages power flow.


Mobile Device Evolution


Mobile Device Architecture Application Layer: Apps and user data. Operating System Layer: Android/iOS file systems. Hardware Layer: NAND chip, SoC, etc. Each layer offers unique data sources for forensics.


Mobile Operating Systems Android: Open-source, Linux-based, file system varies by version. iOS: Proprietary, secure boot chain, file system – APFS. Windows Mobile: Outdated but encountered in legacy cases. BlackBerry OS: Legacy OS with secure messaging.


Smart Cards in Mobile Devices SIM cards are smart cards used in GSM networks. Store IMSI, authentication keys, and SMS. Accessing SIM data requires specific tools and permissions.


SIM vs USIM SIM: Used in 2G/3G networks, limited storage. USIM: Used in 3G/4G/5G, better encryption and storage. Essential for accessing network credentials and call logs.


SIM File Management Files organized as Master File (MF), Dedicated Files (DF), and Elementary Files (EF). EFs store SMS, contacts, and other data. Some files are protected and need authentication to access.


SIM/USIM Security PIN: Personal Identification Number. PUK: Unlock code for blocked SIM. Authentication uses challenge-response with A3/A8 algorithms. Forensic tools must handle locked or encrypted SIMs.


Chapter_2_Mobile_Forensics_Process.pptx
Chapter 2 Mobile Forensics Process
Index 2.1. Mobile Forensic and its Challenges. 2.2. Mobile Forensics Process 2.3. Acquisition Methods 2.4. Emerging Techniques in Mobile Forensics
Introduction to Mobile Forensics Mobile forensics is a specialized branch of digital forensics that deals with the scientific extraction, preservation, analysis, and presentation of evidence from mobile devices in a forensically sound manner. As mobile phones, smartphones, tablets, and other portable devices become integral to daily life, they increasingly serve as rich repositories of digital evidence relevant to various types of investigations, including criminal, civil, and corporate cases.
2.1 Mobile Forensic Challenges Mobile forensics presents several unique and evolving challenges that distinguish it from traditional computer forensics: Device Diversity: Vast Number of Models: Hundreds of manufacturers produce thousands of mobile device models, each with distinct hardware, firmware, and internal structures. Operating System Fragmentation: While Android and iOS dominate, varying versions, custom ROMs (Android), and proprietary operating systems (e.g., feature phones) create inconsistencies. Hardware Variations: Different chipsets (Qualcomm, MediaTek, Apple A-series), memory types (eMMC, UFS), and connectivity options require specialized tools and techniques. Rapid Technological Advancements: Short Lifespan: New device models and OS versions are released frequently, often making forensic tools quickly obsolete. Evolving Security Features: Manufacturers constantly enhance security (e.g., stronger encryption, secure boot, hardware-backed security modules, anti-forensics features), making data access more difficult. Data Volatility: Live Data: Information like running processes, active network connections, and temporary files are highly volatile and can be lost if not preserved quickly and correctly. Overwriting: Constant writes to flash memory (e.g., app updates, new messages) can quickly overwrite deleted data, reducing recovery chances.
Cont. Encryption and Device Locks: Full-Disk Encryption (FDE) and File-Based Encryption (FBE): Modern smartphones typically encrypt user data by default, rendering data unreadable without the correct passcode or biometric unlock. Passcodes and Biometrics: Screen locks, PINs, patterns, fingerprints, and face recognition prevent unauthorized access and complicate acquisition. Secure Boot and Hardware-Backed Keys : These mechanisms make it difficult to bypass OS security or extract encryption keys. Anti-Forensics Techniques: Users can employ methods to hinder forensic analysis, such as wiping data, factory resetting, using encrypted messaging apps, or physically damaging the device. Lack of Standardization: Unlike traditional hard drives, there’s no single standard for mobile device storage, file systems, or communication protocols, requiring tools to adapt to numerous variations. Physical Damage: Devices involved in incidents (e.g., accidents, water damage) may be physically compromised, making data extraction challenging or impossible without specialized repair techniques.
2.2 Mobile Forensics Process The mobile phone evidence extraction process follows a structured methodology to ensure data integrity, admissibility, and comprehensive analysis. This process is generally aligned with the principles of digital forensics: Identification Preservation Acquisition Analysis Reporting
Cont. Identification: Recognize the Need, Identify the Device, Identify Type of Data Preservation: Isolate the Device (Faraday Bag), Document Device State (Record the date, time, battery level, network status), Chain of Custody Acquisition: process of physically or logically extracting data from the mobile device, Tool Selection, Hashing Analysis: Processing the Data, Timeline Reconstruction, Correlation, Validation Reporting: Document Findings, Report Structure, Expert Testimony
Cont. Phase Description Tools Used Preservation Isolate and protect the device Faraday bag, Chain of Custody Form Acquisition Extract data Cellebrite, Magnet AXIOM Analysis Filter and examine data Autopsy, Oxygen, manual review Reporting Create legal documentation HTML/PDF Reports, screenshots
2.3. Acquisition Methods Mobile forensic approaches primarily refer to different methods of data acquisition, ranging from basic manual examination to advanced physical extraction. Manual Extraction (Manual Acquisition): Method: Involves simply using the device’s user interface (UI) to browse and photograph/document visible data (e.g., call logs, messages, contacts displayed on the screen). Pros: Least intrusive, requires no special tools, quick for initial assessment. Cons: Very limited data (only what’s visible), no deleted data recovery, not forensically sound (data can be altered), difficult to scale for large amounts of data. Use Case: Initial triage, quick look at an unlocked device in the field, when other methods are unavailable. Logical Extraction (Logical Acquisition): Method : Acquires data that is logically accessible through the device’s operating system via standard communication protocols (e.g., USB connection, Wi-Fi). This often involves creating a backup of the device. Android : Using ADB (Android Debug Bridge) for backups or pulling specific user-accessible files. iOS : Using iTunes backup functionality. Pros : Generally non-intrusive, preserves data integrity, relatively quick, recovers a good amount of user data (call logs, SMS, contacts, app data from standard locations). Cons : Does not recover deleted data or data from inaccessible areas of the file system, requires the device to be unlocked or trusted by the computer, dependent on OS version and backup capabilities. Tools : Magnet AXIOM, Cellebrite UFED, Oxygen Forensic Detective, ADB. Use Case : Most common and preferred method when possible, quick triage, initial data acquisition from unlocked devices.
Cont. File System Extraction (Filesystem Acquisition): Method : A more comprehensive logical extraction that acquires the entire accessible file system of the device, often including system files and deeper application data that might not be part of a standard logical backup. This often involves exploiting vulnerabilities or using specialized agents. Android : Can be achieved via ADB with root access, custom recovery images (TWRP), or specific forensic tools that bypass OS restrictions. iOS : Possible on jailbroken devices or via specific exploits on un-jailbroken devices (e.g., checkm8 exploit for some iPhones). Pros : Recovers more data than logical extraction, including some deleted files (if not overwritten) and detailed application databases. Cons : More complex, may require device rooting/jailbreaking (which can alter the device), still limited by OS security layers, may not recover truly deleted data from underlying flash memory. Tools : Advanced features of Magnet AXIOM, Cellebrite UFED, Oxygen Forensic Detective. Use Case : When deeper application data or potentially deleted files are required beyond what logical extraction offers. Physical Extraction (Physical Acquisition): Method : The most comprehensive but also the most invasive method. It involves creating a bit-for-bit copy of the device’s internal memory (flash memory). Pros : Recovers the maximum amount of data, including deleted files, unallocated space, and low-level system data; bypasses OS and encryption if done correctly and keys can be derived. Cons : Highly intrusive, may render the device inoperable, requires specialized equipment and expertise, time-consuming, expensive, and can potentially damage evidence if not performed meticulously. Tools : Specialized hardware stations (e.g., ZRT, PC-3000 Flash), chip readers. Use Case : When logical or file system extractions are not possible (e.g., damaged device, strong encryption, highly targeted data recovery), or when the most complete data set, including deleted data, is crucial.
Cont. JTAG and Chip-Off Acquisition: JTAG (Joint Test Action Group) : Connects to test points on the motherboard to extract memory non-destructively. Chip-off: Physically removes the memory chip and reads it using specialized hardware. Used when the device is damaged, locked, or wiped. Risky, requires expertise, but offers deep data recovery.
2.4. Emerging Techniques in Mobile Forensics Cloud Forensics: Extracting data from online services (Google Drive, iCloud). IoT Device Forensics: Handling smartwatches, wearables, and smart home apps. AI-based analysis: Automatically flagging suspicious chats, content, or behavior . Live forensics: Capturing volatile data from running devices before shutdown. Mobile Malware Forensics: Detecting and analyzing malicious code within apps. Encrypted App Recovery: Bypassing or decrypting data from apps like Signal, Telegram.
Chapter_3_Mobile_Device_Forensics.pptx
Chapter 3: Mobile Device Forensics
Introduction Each mobile OS has a unique architecture, security model, and data storage approach, directly impacting forensic methodologies. Understanding these differences is fundamental. Android : Open-source OS, supports rooting, app logs, SQLite databases. iOS : Encrypted file system, requires jailbreaking for deeper access. BlackBerry : Legacy secure OS, supports PIN messages and encrypted data. Windows Mobile : Less common today, uses NTFS/FAT file system.
3.1 Mobile OS Forensics Android Forensics Architecture & Characteristics: Linux Kernel-based: Open-source, highly customizable. Android Runtime (ART): Executes app code. App Sandboxing : Each app runs in its own isolated process. File System : Typically ext4 or f2fs. User data often in /data/data/< package_name > (app-specific) and / sdcard (user-accessible). Device Fragmentation : Wide variety of manufacturers, models, and Android versions Security Model: App Permissions : Granular control over resources. Full-Disk Encryption (FDE) / File-Based Encryption (FBE): Default on modern devices. Verified Boot, SELinux . Forensic Implications: Acquisition Challenges : FBE makes data inaccessible without passcode when locked. Rooting might be needed for full filesystem access (but alters device). Data Locations : Standardized app data locations (SQLite databases) are common. Tool Support : Wide range of commercial and open-source tools due to its open nature.
Cont. iOS Forensics Architecture & Characteristics: Unix-like (Darwin Kernel): Closed-source, tightly integrated with Apple hardware. Secure Enclave: Hardware-based security for cryptographic keys and biometrics. APFS (Apple File System): Modern file system. Strict Sandboxing: Apps are heavily restricted. Security Model: Hardware Encryption: Always-on encryption tied to user passcode. Data Protection Classes: Different levels of encryption for files based on access patterns. Activation Lock: Anti-theft feature. Code Signing: All apps must be signed by Apple. Forensic Implications: High Security: Very challenging when locked due to strong encryption and Secure Enclave. Limited Access: Reliance on iTunes backups for logical acquisition. Full filesystem often requires jailbreaking (alters device) or specific hardware exploits (e.g., checkm8). Data Sources: iTunes backups, iCloud backups, specific hardware extractions. Tool Support: Primarily commercial tools, some open-source for specific vulnerabilities/jailbreaks.
Cont. BlackBerry Forensics Legacy Systems (BlackBerry OS 7 and older): Proprietary OS: Not Android or iOS. Strong Encryption: Often had robust device encryption. BlackBerry Desktop Manager: Primary tool for logical backups. Artifacts: BBM messages, email, calendar, contacts. Forensic Implications: Declining Relevance: Less common in modern investigations. Tool Support: Older commercial tools may support, but limited new development. Proprietary Formats: Requires specialized parsers.
Cont. Windows Mobile Forensics Windows Phone (Windows CE/Mobile, Windows Phone 7/8/10 Mobile): Microsoft OS: Less prevalent in the market. Live Tiles Interface. Integration with Microsoft Services: OneDrive, Outlook. Forensic Implications: Limited Market Share: Infrequently encountered in modern cases. Acquisition: Often relied on logical backups via Zune software (older) or MTP/PTP protocols. Artifacts: SMS, call logs, contacts, browser history (IE/Edge). Tool Support: Limited compared to Android/iOS.
3.2 Artefact Extraction Digital artifacts are pieces of data left behind by user activity or system processes that can be used as evidence. These artifacts help reconstruct events, establish timelines, identify individuals, and prove intent.
Cont. Contacts and Phone Call Artefacts Forensic Value: Identity: Who the user communicates with. Associations: Links between individuals. Communication Patterns: Frequency, duration of calls. Timelines: Exact timestamps of calls. Typical Locations: Android: SQLite databases /data/data/ com.android.providers.contacts /databases/contacts2.db , /data/data/ com.android.providers.contacts /databases/ calllog.db iOS: SQLite databases /private/var/mobile/Library/ AddressBook / AddressBook.sqlitedb , /private/var/wireless/Library/ CallHistory / call_history.db Cloud Sync: Google Contacts, iCloud Contacts. SIM Card: Limited contact storage (EF_ADN) and last dialed numbers. Extraction Methods: Logical backup, filesystem acquisition, physical acquisition, SIM card readers. Tools: Commercial forensic suites (AXIOM, UFED, Oxygen), SQLite browsers, ADB
Cont. SMS Artefacts Forensic Value: Direct Communication: Content of conversations. Timelines: Exact timestamps of messages sent/received. Participants: Sender and receiver phone numbers. Multimedia: Attached images, audio, video in MMS. Typical Locations: Android: SQLite database /data/data/ com.android.providers.telephony /databases/ mmssms.db iOS (Messages/iMessage): SQLite database /private/var/mobile/Library/SMS/ sms.db SIM Card : Limited SMS storage (EF_SMS). Extraction Methods: Logical backup, filesystem acquisition, physical acquisition, SIM card readers. Tools: Commercial forensic suites, SQLite browsers.
Cont. Network Artefacts Forensic Value: Connectivity: When and where the device connected to networks. Associated Devices: Bluetooth pairings. Web Activity: Websites visited, search queries. Communication: Evidence of data transfer, app usage. Types & Locations: Wi-Fi Connection History: Network SSIDs, MAC addresses, connection times (often in system logs or specific databases). Bluetooth Pairing Records: Paired devices, connection timestamps. Cellular Network Logs: Cell tower IDs, signal strength, network changes Web Browser History: URLs, timestamps, downloads DNS Cache: Recently resolved domain names. Extraction Methods: Logical/filesystem acquisition, physical acquisition. T ools: Commercial forensic suites, browser history parsers, network analysis tools.
Cont. Location Artefacts Forensic Value: Movement Patterns: Where the user has been. Alibi Corroboration/Refutation: Proving or disproving presence at a location. Association: Linking a device to a crime scene. Intent: Showing travel to specific locations. Types & Locations: GPS Logs: Raw GPS coordinates from the device’s GPS receiver (often in system databases or specific app data). Geotagged Media: Photos and videos often embed GPS coordinates in EXIF metadata. Wi-Fi Location: Databases of Wi-Fi access points and their known locations. Cell Tower Location: Records of connected cell towers (less precise, but ubiquitous). Application-Specific Location Data: Google Maps history, Apple Maps history, ride-sharing apps, fitness trackers, social media check-ins. Bluetooth Beaconing: Proximity to known Bluetooth devices. Extraction Methods: Logical/filesystem acquisition, physical acquisition. Tools: Commercial forensic suites, EXIF data viewers, mapping tools (Google Earth).
Cont. System Artefacts Forensic Value: Device Context: What kind of device, OS version, build. User Activity: When the device was used, which apps were opened. Installed Capabilities: What applications were present on the device. Security Posture: Patch level, security settings. Types & Locations: Device Information: IMEI, MEID, Serial Number, Phone Number, OS version, Installed Applications List: List of all apps, their versions, and installation dates. Application Usage Records: When apps were last opened System Logs: Records of system events, errors, crashes, security events User Accounts: Information about configured email, social media, and cloud accounts. Device State: Battery level, network status at specific times. Extraction Methods Logical/filesystem acquisition, physical acquisition. Tools: Commercial forensic suites, log viewers, text editors, custom scripts.
Cont. Multimedia Files Artefacts Forensic Value: Direct Visual/Audio Evidence: Content directly related to the investigation. Context: What was happening, who was present. EXIF Data (for photos): Timestamps, device model, camera settings, GPS coordinates (if enabled). Metadata: Creation/modification dates, file sizes, unique hashes. Typical Locations: Android: / sdcard /DCIM/Camera/, / sdcard /Pictures/, / sdcard /Downloads/, iOS: /private/var/mobile/Media/DCIM/ , /private/var/mobile/Media/ PhotoData / . Cloud Sync: Google Photos, iCloud Photos. Extraction Methods: Logical acquisition (if accessible), filesystem acquisition, physical acquisition. Tools: Commercial forensic suites, image viewers, video players, audio players, EXIF data viewers/extractors.
3.3 Data and File Carving Data and File Carving The process of recovering files or fragments of files from unallocated (free) space on a storage medium. It works by searching for known file headers and footers (signatures) and attempting to reconstruct the data in between. Why it’s needed: Files that have been “deleted” by the OS are often not immediately overwritten. The OS just removes the pointer to the file in the file system table. File carving can recover data from damaged file systems or raw disk images where the file system metadata is corrupted or missing. Process: Acquire a physical or full filesystem image of the mobile device’s storage. Scan the raw data for specific file signatures Extract the data blocks between the identified header and footer. Attempt to reconstruct the file. Limitations: Fragmented files are harder to carve completely. Encryption makes carving impossible without decryption. Wear leveling and garbage collection on flash memory can make recovery difficult or impossible as data is moved/erased. Common Tools: Foremost: Command-line tool for carving various file types. Scalpel: Improved version of Foremost, faster. PhotoRec : Recovers various file types, often used for multimedia.
3.4 Deleted File Recovery Deleted Files Recovery Concept of “Deletion”: When a file is “deleted” by the operating system, its data blocks are not immediately erased. Instead, the file system simply marks the space occupied by the file as “available” or “unallocated.” The data remains until it is overwritten by new data. Why it’s challenging on Mobile Devices (Flash Memory): Wear Leveling: Flash memory (NAND, eMMC, UFS) controllers distribute writes evenly across the memory cells to extend lifespan. This means a “deleted” file’s data might be physically moved to a different location without the OS knowing, or its original location might be quickly overwritten. Garbage Collection (GC): Flash memory controllers periodically consolidate valid data and erase invalid (deleted) data blocks to free up space. This process can permanently erase deleted files. TRIM Command: Modern operating systems send TRIM commands to SSDs/flash memory when files are deleted. This command tells the controller that the data blocks are no longer needed and can be erased, leading to faster and more permanent deletion.
Cont. Methods for Recovery: Physical Acquisition: The most effective method. Creates a bit-for-bit copy of the raw flash memory, allowing carving tools to work on the unallocated space. Filesystem Acquisition: Can sometimes recover recently deleted files if they haven’t been overwritten or garbage collected yet, especially if the file system metadata still points to them. File Carving: Applied to the unallocated space recovered from physical or full filesystem images. Factors Affecting Success: Time Since Deletion: Shorter time, higher chance. Device Usage: Less activity after deletion means less chance of overwriting. TRIM Support: If TRIM is active, recovery likelihood decreases significantly. Flash Memory Type & Controller: Different controllers handle wear leveling/GC differently. Acquisition Method: Physical acquisition offers the best chance.
3.5 Bypassing Security Controls Bypassing Security Controls Purpose: In forensic investigations, bypassing security controls (screen locks, encryption) is often necessary to access evidence. Legal & Ethical: Crucially, such actions must always be performed with proper legal authorization (e.g., search warrant, consent) and within ethical guidelines. Unauthorized bypass attempts are illegal. Risks: Improper bypass attempts can lead to data loss, device damage, or alteration of evidence.
Chapter_4_Mobile_Forensics_Tools.pptx
Chapter 4: Mobile Forensics Tools Overview of tools used in mobile forensics investigations
Introduction to Mobile Forensics Tools Why Specialized Tools? Complexity of mobile OS (Android, iOS). Proprietary file systems and data structures. Encryption and security measures. Need for forensically sound acquisition. Vast amount and variety of data. Categories of Tools: Commercial Tools: Generally all-in-one solutions with broad device support, advanced extraction, decoding, and reporting capabilities. Require licensing. Open-Source Tools: Free, often command-line based, may require more technical expertise, but highly customizable and valuable for specific tasks. Hardware Tools: For physical extraction (e.g., JTAG, Chip-Off). Software Tools: For logical, filesystem, and limited physical extractions.
4.1 Cellebrite Cellebrite is a global leader in digital intelligence solutions, widely used by law enforcement, military, intelligence agencies, and corporate investigators. Cellebrite offers a comprehensive suite of tools, with UFED (Universal Forensic Extraction Device) being their flagship for mobile forensics. Features of Cellebrite UFED Physical Analyzer Comprehensive Data Extraction: Physical Extraction: Bit-for-bit copies of data from the device, including unallocated space. Often bypasses locks and encryption. File System Extraction: Accesses the logical file structure of the device. Logical Extraction: Acquires user-level data (contacts, SMS, call logs, photos) via device APIs or backups (e.g., iTunes backups). Advanced Decoding & Parsing: Automatically decodes and presents data from various mobile OS. Parses data from thousands of applications (e.g., WhatsApp, Signal, Facebook, Snapchat). Recovers deleted data (SMS, contacts, call logs, photos) through carving and database analysis. Decryption capabilities for encrypted backups and some devices (dependent on specific device/OS versions). Analysis & Visualization Tools: Timeline View: Reconstructs events chronologically across different data types. Link Analysis: Visualizes connections between contacts, calls, messages. Geolocational Analysis: Maps locations from various sources (GPS, Wi-Fi, cell towers, geotagged media). Watch Lists/Keyword Search: Automates searching for specific terms or identifying persons of interest. Image & Video Categorization: AI-powered classification of media content. SQLite Wizard & Hex Viewer: For in-depth manual analysis of databases and raw data. Reporting: Generates comprehensive and customizable reports in various formats (PDF, HTML, XML, Excel) for legal proceedings. Integrations: Integrates with other Cellebrite products like UFED Cloud Analyzer (for cloud data) and Pathfinder (for advanced intelligence analysis).
Usage Acquisition Process: Device Connection: Connect the mobile device to the UFED via cable. Selection: Choose the device model and desired extraction method (logical Bypass/Unlock (if necessary): UFED attempts to bypass screen locks Data Extraction: The tool performs the chosen extraction. Forensic Image Creation: A forensically sound image is created. Analysis Workflow: Import Data: Load the extracted image into UFED Physical Analyzer. Automatic Decoding: The software automatically decodes recognized artifacts. Review Data: Navigate through categories (calls, messages, apps, locations). Search & Filter: Apply keywords, date ranges, or other filters. Advanced Analysis: Use timeline, link analysis, or carving features. Reporting: Generate reports based on findings. User Base: Primarily used by law enforcement, military, intelligence, and large corporate investigative units due to its comprehensive capabilities and cost.
Supported Devices Broadest Support in the Industry: Supports thousands of mobile devices: Smartphones, feature phones, GPS devices, tablets, drones. Covers major operating systems: Android (vast range of manufacturers like Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi, etc.), Apple iOS (iPhones, iPads, iPod Touch), BlackBerry, Windows Mobile, Symbian, Palm OS. Continuous Updates: Cellebrite is known for frequent updates to support newly released devices and OS versions, as well as new applications and security bypasses. Specific Access Levels: Support varies by device and OS version (e.g., full file system extraction for some Androids, advanced logical for newer iOS, physical for older/vulnerable devices).
4.2 Oxygen Forensics Suite Oxygen Forensics is another leading developer of mobile and cloud forensics software, offering comprehensive tools for digital investigations. Features of Oxygen Forensics Suite Multi-Source Data Extraction: Mobile & IoT Devices: Logical, file system, and physical extraction from smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, drones, etc. Cloud Services: Connects to over 100 cloud services (e.g., Google, iCloud, WhatsApp, Instagram, Telegram) with legal authorization to extract data. Computer Forensics: Extracts artifacts from Windows, macOS, and Linux machines (e.g., web browser data, system files, credentials). Backup & Image Import: Imports iTunes backups, Android backups, raw disk images, and extractions from other forensic tools. Advanced Data Decoding & Analysis: App Data Parsing: Supports over 50,000 app versions, including social media, messaging, navigation, and gaming apps. Deleted Data Recovery: Advanced algorithms to recover deleted messages, contacts, files, and more. Encryption Bypass & Password Recovery: Tools to bypass screen locks, decrypt encrypted backups, and recover passwords. Malware Detection: Identifies malicious applications or artifacts. Integrated Analytical Tools: Timeline: Consolidates events from various sources into a unified chronological view. Link Analysis: Visualizes communication networks and social connections. Mapping: Plots geo-coordinates from all extracted sources on maps. Image & Video Categorization: AI-powered media analysis, including facial recognition and object detection. Key Evidence Identification: Highlights critical artifacts and insights. SQLite Viewer, Plist Viewer, Hex Viewer: For in-depth examination. Reporting: Customizable reports in multiple formats (PDF, HTML, XML, CSV). Enterprise Solutions: Offers multi-user, server-based licenses for larger organizations with remote access capabilities.
Usage Flexible Acquisition: Connect Device/Select Source: Choose the mobile device, cloud service, computer, or an existing backup/image. Extraction Method: Select the appropriate extraction method (e.g., “Physical,” “File System,” “iOS Agent,” “iTunes Backup,” “Cloud Extractor”). Process: The tool guides through the acquisition, potentially requiring device interaction or credentials for cloud services. Analysis Workflow: Data Loading: Once extracted, data is loaded into the intuitive GUI. Automatic Parsing: Data is automatically parsed and categorized. Forensic Explorer: Browse through different data categories. Advanced Analysis Features: Utilize timeline, link analysis, maps, and media categorization to identify connections and patterns. Filtering & Search: Efficiently filter and search across all data. Report Generation: Create detailed reports for documentation and presentation. User Base: Law enforcement, corporate investigators, private forensic specialists, and government agencies worldwide.
Supported Devices Extensive Device and OS Support : Android : Wide range of manufacturers and chipsets (MediaTek, UNISOC, Qualcomm, Samsung Exynos , Huawei Kirin, Sony). Offers physical, full file system, application downgrade, and Android Agent extractions. iOS : iPhones, iPads. Supports iOS Agent (for full file system/keychain on specific iOS versions), iTunes backups, and Checkm8 exploit-based extractions (for older devices). Feature phones, smartwatches, drones, etc. Cloud Services : 100+ cloud services supported (WhatsApp, Telegram, iCloud, Google, Facebook, etc.). Computer Systems : Windows, macOS, Linux for local artifact extraction. Regular Updates : Provides frequent updates to maintain compatibility with new devices, OS versions, and application updates.
4.3 Paraben iRecovery Stick Designed as a simpler, more user-friendly tool primarily for iOS device data recovery, including deleted data. Often marketed towards consumers and smaller investigative units. A USB stick containing the software. Features of Paraben iRecovery Stick Data Recovery Focus: Recovers existing and deleted data: SMS/iMessages, call history, contacts, web history, calendar, notes, photos (including hidden photos from specific apps), voice memos, map history. Specializes in recovering data from various popular messaging and social media apps (e.g., WhatsApp, Gmail, Kik, Twitter, Facebook Messenger). User-Friendly Interface: Designed for ease of use, often with a simple “connect and click” operation. Stealth Operation: Runs directly from the USB stick, aiming to leave no trace on the computer or the phone itself (though any acquisition inherently interacts with the device). iTunes Backup Analysis: Can analyze and recover data directly from iTunes backup files, even if the physical phone is not present. Hidden Photo Recovery: Claims to recover photos hidden in over 30 popular “photo hiding” apps. Basic Analysis: Provides keyword search functionality and can generate basic reports (e.g., Excel format). Lifetime Updates: Typically includes free lifetime software updates for compatibility with new iOS versions.
Usage Simple Process: Connect : Plug the iRecovery Stick into a Windows computer. Connect Device : Connect the iPhone/iPad to the same computer using its compatible data cable. Launch Software : Run the software directly from the stick. Initiate Recovery : Click “Start” or “Recover.” Review Results : The software presents the recovered data in an organized, readable format. Prerequisites : For direct device access, the device usually needs to be unlocked, and iTunes trust established. It generally cannot bypass screen locks or device encryption.
Supported Devices iOS Devices: Primarily supports Apple iPhones, iPads, and iPod Touch devices. iOS Versions: Generally aims to support current and recent iOS versions (e.g., up to iOS 17.x as per recent marketing). Focus: Its strength is in logical data extraction and deleted data recovery from SQLite databases and specific app structures, rather than deep physical acquisition from locked or highly encrypted devices. Limitations: Does not perform physical acquisition from raw memory chips. Its capabilities are dependent on Apple’s security updates and whether it can access data via software means.
4.4 Open-Source Mobile Forensics Tools Autopsy: Extensible forensic platform with mobile modules. MobSF : Dynamic/static analysis of Android and iOS apps. ADB (Android Debug Bridge): Basic tool for Android data extraction. Volatility Framework: An open-source memory forensics framework. ExifTool: Extracting EXIF data from photos and videos (timestamps, GPS coordinates, camera model), which is crucial for mobile forensics.
Enrichment: Fact Checks & Extra Info (2025 Trends)


                  
                  Mobile Forensics Trends (2025) 
                  
                


iOS vs Android:

iOS: Secure Enclave and strictly controlled ecosystem make extraction hard.
Android: Fragmentation (many versions/models) requires diverse tools.


App Encryption: WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram use end-to-end encryption, challenging standard extraction.
Cloud Sync: Data is increasingly stored in iCloud/Google Drive, requiring cloud forensics.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Cyber Crime and Cyber Security
Subject: Cyber Law (CDS-362)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: cyber-law cybercrime security-policy CIA-triad vulnerabilities

1.1 Introduction
The rapid expansion of the Internet has brought both efficiency and risk. Cybercrime has emerged as a major threat, leveraging technology to commit fraud, theft, and sabotage. Cyber Security is the discipline responsible for protecting assets from these threats.

1.2 Cybercrime: Definition and Origin

Definition: Any illegal activity carried out using a computer, network, or digital device. The computer can be the tool (used to attack others) or the target (the victim of the attack).
Origin: The term “Cyber Crime” is linked to the evolution of the internet and digital systems, where traditional crimes (theft, fraud) migrated to the digital domain.


1.3 Cybercrime vs. Information Security

Cybercrime: The offense. The act of violating laws using digital means.
Information Security (InfoSec): The defense. The practice of protecting information by mitigating information risks.


1.4 Classifications of Cybercrimes
Cybercrimes are often categorized by their target:
1.4.1 Crimes Against Individuals

E-Mail Spoofing: Forging the email header to make it appear as if it came from a legitimate source.
Spamming: Sending unsolicited bulk messages.
Cyber Defamation: Publishing slanderous or libelous information about a person online to damage their reputation.
Cyber Stalking: Use of the internet to harass or stalk a victim.

1.4.2 Crimes Against Property

Internet Time Theft: Unauthorized use of someone else’s internet minutes (older concept from dial-up days, now relates to Wi-Fi theft).
Data Diddling: Changing data before or during entry into a computer system.

Example: A clerk changes a deposit amount from 1000 to 100 before typing it in, stealing the difference.


Salami Attack (Salami Slicing): Stealing tiny, unnoticeable amounts of money from many accounts.

Example: Rounding down interest rates and transferring the fractions of a cent to the attacker’s account.


Forgery: Altering digital documents to deceive.

1.4.3 Crimes Against Organizations/Society

Web Jacking: Forcefully taking control of a website (often by DNS poisoning) to redirect users to a fake site.
Industrial Espionage: Stealing trade secrets or intellectual property from competitors.
Computer Sabotage: Deliberately destroying hardware or software.
Email Bombing: Overwhelming an inbox with massive amounts of email to cause a DoS.


1.5 Introduction to Cyber Security
Definition: The body of technologies, processes, and practices designed to protect networks, devices, programs, and data from attack, damage, or unauthorized access.
1.5.1 The CIA Triad
The three pillars of Information Security:

Confidentiality: Ensuring data is accessible only to authorized users (preventing leaks).

Controls: Encryption, Access Control Lists (ACLs).


Integrity: Ensuring data is accurate and not tampered with.

Controls: Hashing, Digital Signatures.


Availability: Ensuring systems and data are available when needed.

Controls: Redundancy, Backups, DDoS protection.




1.6 Vulnerability, Threat, and Harmful Acts
Understanding the relationship is key to risk management.

























TermDefinitionAnalogyVulnerabilityA weakness or gap in protection.An unlocked door.ThreatA potential danger that exploits a vulnerability.A burglar.Harmful ActThe actual realization of the threat (Attack).The burglar opening the door and stealing.
Formula:
Risk = Threat \times Vulnerability \times Impact

1.7 Cyber Security Policy
A Security Policy is a formal document outlining how an organization protects its assets. It defines the rules, responsibilities, and acceptable use of technology.
1.7.1 Domains of Cyber Security Policy
Policies typically cover these key domains:

Physical Security: Protecting the hardware (servers, locks, cameras).
Network Security: Firewalls, VPNs, Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS).
User Access Control (IAM): Identification, Authentication, and Authorization.
Incident Response: How the organization reacts to a breach.
Disaster Recovery: How to restore operations after a major failure.

Chapter 2: Cybercrimes and Cybersecurity: The Legal Perspectives
Subject: Cyber Law (CDS-362)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: IT-Act-2000 IT-Act-2008 digital-signature cyber-law legal

2.1 Introduction
Cyber laws are essential to regulate the digital ecosystem, providing legal recognition for electronic transactions and defining penalties for cybercrimes.
2.2 Why Do We Need Cyberlaws: The Indian Context

e-Commerce Growth: To facilitate secure online business.
e-Governance: To enable digital filing of government documents.
Evidence: To make electronic records admissible as evidence in court.


2.3 The Indian IT Act, 2000
Enacted on October 17, 2000, it is the primary law in India dealing with cybercrime and electronic commerce.

Objective: To provide legal recognition for transactions carried out by means of electronic data interchange (EDI).

2.3.1 Key Sections

Section 3: Electronic authentication of records via Digital Signatures.
Section 43: Penalty for damage to computer systems (e.g., unauthorized access, downloading data, introducing viruses).
Section 65: Tampering with computer source documents.
Section 66: Hacking with computer system (Generic cybercrime section).
Section 67: Publishing obscene information in electronic form.


2.4 Digital Signatures and the Indian IT Act
The Act distinguishes between “Electronic Signatures” and “Digital Signatures”.






























FeatureDigital Signature (Sec 3)Electronic Signature (Sec 3A)TechnologyUses Asymmetric Cryptography (Public/Private Key).Any electronic method (e.g., scanned signature, checkbox, Aadhaar eSign).SecurityHigh. Tamper-proof.Low to Medium.VerificationVerified using the signer’s Public Key.Verified by the specific method used.AuthorityIssued by a Certifying Authority (CA).Can be self-generated or third-party.

2.5 Amendments to the Indian IT Act (2008)
The Information Technology (Amendment) Act, 2008 focused on data privacy, information security, and defining new crimes.
2.5.1 Key Additions

Section 66A: Punishment for sending offensive messages (Repealed by Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal Case for violating Free Speech).
Section 66F: Cyber Terrorism. Acts intended to threaten the unity/integrity of India. Punishment: Life Imprisonment.
Section 43A: Compensation for failure to protect data (Data Privacy). Mandates reasonable security practices for corporates.


2.6 Challenges to Indian Law

Jurisdiction: Cybercrime is borderless; Indian laws apply to computers in India, but enforcing them on foreign servers in the US/Europe is difficult (MLAT treaties required).
Encryption: Law enforcement struggles to decrypt data from apps like WhatsApp (End-to-End Encryption).
Anonymity: Use of VPNs and TOR makes attribution hard.


2.7 Cybercrime and Punishment






























OffenseSectionPunishmentHackingSec 663 Years Imprisonment + ₹5 Lakh fineIdentity TheftSec 66C3 Years + ₹1 LakhCyber TerrorismSec 66FLife ImprisonmentViolation of PrivacySec 66E3 Years + ₹2 Lakh
