Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Cyber-Law/Notes/C.content:
Chapter 3: Cybersecurity: Organizational Implications
Subject: Cyber Law (CDS-362)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: organizational-security IPR social-media incident-handling cost-of-cybercrime

3.1 Cost of Cybercrimes
Cyberattacks cause massive financial and reputational damage to organizations.
Types of Costs:

Direct Financial Loss: Theft of funds (e.g., banking trojans) or Ransomware payments.
Operational Disruption: Downtime where the business cannot function (DoS attacks).
Legal & Regulatory Costs: Fines for non-compliance (e.g., GDPR, IT Act Section 43A) and lawsuits from affected customers.
Reputational Damage: Loss of customer trust, which is often harder to recover than money.


3.2 Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) in Cyberspace
Intellectual Property (IP) refers to creations of the mind (software, designs, content).

Cyber Theft: Stealing trade secrets or source code.
Software Piracy: Illegal copying and distribution of software.
Copyright Infringement: Hosting copyrighted movies/music on a server without permission.
Cybersquatting: Registering a domain name (e.g., google-verify.com) aimed at misleading users or selling it back to the trademark owner at a premium.


3.3 Security and Privacy in Cloud Computing
Moving to the cloud (AWS/Azure) introduces new risks.

Shared Responsibility: The cloud provider secures the infrastructure, but the organization must secure the data.
Data Sovereignty: If data is stored on a server in another country, foreign laws may apply.
Privacy Concerns: Risk of data leakage in multi-tenant environments (where multiple customers share the same hardware).


3.4 Social Media Marketing & Risks
Social media is a double-edged sword for organizations.

Risks:

Brand Hijacking: Attackers creating fake profiles to impersonate the company.
Phishing: Attackers posting malicious links in comments or DMs.
Information Leakage: Employees accidentally sharing sensitive internal info in photos or posts.


Guidelines: Companies need a strict Social Media Policy defining what employees can and cannot post.


3.5 Incident Handling
Incident Response (IR) is the organized approach to addressing and managing the aftermath of a security breach.
NIST IR Life Cycle:

Preparation: Policy, Tools, Team training.
Detection & Analysis: Monitoring logs (SIEM), verifying alerts.
Containment, Eradication, & Recovery:

Containment: Isolating the infected system.
Eradication: Removing the malware/patching the flaw.
Recovery: Restoring data from backups and bringing systems back online.


Post-Incident Activity: “Lessons Learned” meeting to improve future response.


3.6 Organizational Guidelines for Safe Computing
To mitigate risks, organizations enforce specific policies:

Acceptable Use Policy (AUP): Rules for using company internet and devices (e.g., “No gambling sites”, “No personal USB drives”).
Password Policy: Mandatory complexity (e.g., 12 chars, special symbols) and rotation.
Clean Desk Policy: ensuring sensitive papers/USBs are not left on desks.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Cyber-Law/Notes/C.title: Chapter 4 - Information Security Policies
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Cyber-Law/Notes/C.content:
Chapter 4: Information Security Policies
Subject: Cyber Law (CDS-362)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: security-policy tiered-policies duty-of-care duty-of-loyalty compliance

4.1 Introduction
An Information Security Policy (ISP) is a document that directs the behavior of employees regarding the protection of the organization’s information assets. It acts as the “Constitution” for security within a company.

4.2 Corporate Policy Hierarchy (Tiers)
Policies are typically organized into three tiers to separate high-level goals from technical details.
4.2.1 Tier 1: Organization-wide (Enterprise) Policy

Purpose: Sets the strategic direction, scope, and tone for all security efforts.
Audience: All employees, stakeholders, and third parties.
Characteristics: Broad, rarely changes, signed by the CEO/Board.
Example: “The organization values data privacy and will comply with all applicable laws.”

4.2.2 Tier 2: Issue-Specific Policies

Purpose: Address specific areas of technology or behavior.
Audience: Users of that specific technology.
Examples:

Acceptable Use Policy (AUP): Rules for internet/email use.
Access Control Policy: Who gets access to what data.
Network Security Policy: Rules for VPNs and Firewalls.



4.2.3 Tier 3: System-Specific Policies (Procedures/Standards)

Purpose: Technical specifications and step-by-step instructions.
Audience: IT admins, technicians, developers.
Examples:

Firewall Configuration Standards (Which ports to block).
Server Hardening Guidelines (How to secure a Linux server).




4.3 Legal Requirements
Security policies are not just best practices; they are often legally mandated.
4.3.1 Duty of Care
The legal obligation to potential victims (customers/employees) to take “reasonable” steps to prevent harm.

In InfoSec: Organizations must implement standard security measures (Firewalls, Encryption) to prevent data breaches. Failure to do so is “Negligence”.

4.3.2 Duty of Loyalty
A fiduciary duty owed by employees (especially executives) to act in the best interest of the organization.

In InfoSec: Employees must not misuse company data for personal gain (e.g., selling trade secrets, insider trading).

4.3.3 Other Regulations

GDPR: Requires policies for data privacy.
HIPAA: Requires policies for healthcare data.
Indian IT Act (Sec 43A): Requires “Reasonable Security Practices”.


4.4 Business Requirements
Policies must align with business goals, not hinder them.

Cost: Security controls shouldn’t cost more than the value of the asset being protected.
Productivity: Policies shouldn’t be so strict that employees can’t do their jobs.
Reputation: Policies help maintain customer trust.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Cyber-Law/Notes/C.content:
Chapter 5: Planning and Preparation
Subject: Cyber Law (CDS-362)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: policy-development planning risk-assessment team-roles

5.1 Introduction
Before writing a single word of a security policy, extensive planning is required. A policy that isn’t planned well will be ignored or resented by employees.

5.2 Information Security Policy Development Lifecycle
Developing a policy is a continuous cycle, not a one-time event.

Risk Assessment: Identify what needs protecting (Assets) and what threatens it.
Policy Construction: Drafting the policy with input from stakeholders.
Publication (Implementation): Distributing the policy to all employees.
Adoption: Training employees and enforcing the rules.
Review (Maintenance): Updating the policy annually or after a major change (e.g., new technology, new laws).


5.3 Preparation Activities

Establish Goals: Why are we writing this? (e.g., “To comply with GDPR” or “To stop data leaks”).
Check Legal Requirements: Ensure the policy doesn’t violate labor laws or privacy regulations.
Cost-Benefit Analysis: Will the cost of enforcing the policy (e.g., blocking USB drives) outweigh the benefit?


5.4 Team Composition (Roles)
Policy development is a group effort.

Management/Leadership: Provides the authority and budget. Their visible support is crucial.
Information Security Team: The subject matter experts who define what needs security.
Legal Counsel: Ensures the wording is legally sound and enforceable.
Human Resources (HR): Handles the disciplinary actions if the policy is violated.
Focus Groups: Small groups of employees from different departments (e.g., Sales, IT, Finance) who review the draft to ensure it is practical and understandable.


5.5 Policy Writer and Editor Characteristics

Writer: Needs to be a Generalist who understands both tech and business. Must write in “Plain English” (avoiding jargon) so that non-technical staff can understand.
Editor: Ensuring consistency, proper grammar, and clarity. They act as the “First Reader”.


5.6 Development Checklist

 Has the risk assessment been completed?
 Have we identified the target audience?
 Is the management on board?
 Do we have a template?

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Cyber-Law/Notes/C.content:
Chapter 6: Developing Policies
Subject: Cyber Law (CDS-362)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: policy-development security-policy RFC2196

6.1 Introduction
The Security Policy is the cornerstone of an organization’s security program. It defines the “What” via broad statements.

Analogy: If a Standard is the speed limit (e.g., 60 km/h) and a Procedure is how to drive the car, the Policy is the law stating “You must drive safely”.

6.2 Key Elements of a Policy
Every policy document should contain the following sections:

Overview: A brief summary of the policy’s intent.
Purpose: Why is this policy being created? (e.g., “To protect customer credit card data”).
Scope: Who and what does this cover? (e.g., “All employees in the Sales department”, “All laptops owned by the company”).
Target Audience: Who is responsible for reading and following it?
Policy Statement: The actual rule (e.g., “All passwords must be changed every 90 days”).
Definitions: Explaining technical terms (e.g., “Two-Factor Authentication”).
Enforcement/Sanctions: What happens if you break the rule? (e.g., “Termination of employment”, “Legal action”).


6.3 Policy Format
Policies should be consistent in look and feel.

Version Control: Tracking changes (e.g., v1.0, v1.1).
Effective Date: When does the rule start?
Review Date: When will it be checked for relevance?
Approver: Name/Title of the executive who signed it off.


6.4 Why Implement a Policy?

Liability: Reduces legal risks (Due Diligence).
Consistency: Ensures everyone follows the same rules.
Guidance: Helps employees make secure decisions without asking IT every time.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Cyber-Law/Notes/C.content:
Chapter 7: Developing Standards
Subject: Cyber Law (CDS-362)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: standards ISO27001 NIST compliance

7.1 Introduction
While a Policy is a high-level statement of intent (“We will use strong passwords”), a Standard defines the specific, mandatory requirements to meet that intent (“Passwords must be 12 characters long”).

7.2 What Does a Standard Look Like?
Standards are more technical and rigid than policies.

Technology Specific: e.g., “All Windows 10 machines must have BitLocker enabled.”
Metric Driven: e.g., “Encryption must use AES-256.”


7.3 Where Do I Get Standards?
Organizations rarely invent standards from scratch. They adopt industry best practices.

ISO/IEC 27001: The international standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS).
NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology): US government standards (e.g., NIST SP 800-53).
PCI-DSS: Standards for handling credit card data.
CIS Benchmarks: Technical settings for hardening operating systems (Windows, Linux).


7.4 Sample Information Security Manual
An IS Manual often aggregates all standards into one place.

Workstation Standard:

Screen lock timeout: 5 minutes.
Antivirus: Always updated.
USB Ports: Disabled by default.


Server Standard:

Root login: Disabled via SSH.
Logs: Retained for 1 year.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Cyber-Law/Notes/C.title: Chapter 8 - Developing Procedures
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Cyber-Law/Notes/C.content:
Chapter 8: Developing Procedures
Subject: Cyber Law (CDS-362)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: procedures SOP documentation workflows

8.1 Introduction
Procedures (or SOPs - Standard Operating Procedures) are the step-by-step instructions on HOW to perform a task to comply with a Policy and Standard.

Hierarchy: Policy (Why) → Standard (What) → Procedure (How).


8.2 Important Procedure Requirements

Clarity: Must be understood by the person performing the task (e.g., a junior sysadmin).
Reproducibility: If two people follow the procedure, they should get the same result.
Currency: Must be updated whenever the software/process changes.


8.3 Key Elements in Procedure Writing

Action Steps: Numbered steps (1, 2, 3…).
Screenshots: Visual aids to avoid confusion.
Warnings: “Do not click this” or “This will reboot the server”.
Rollback Plan: What to do if the procedure fails.


8.4 Procedure Checklist

 Is the starting state defined? (e.g., “Server must be powered on”).
 Are the tools listed? (e.g., “You need Admin rights”).
 Is the output defined? (e.g., “The service will show status: Running”).


8.5 Procedure Development Review
Procedures should be tested (“Walked through”) by someone other than the author to find gaps or confusing steps. This is often called a Tabletop Exercise or Dry Run.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.title: Chapter 1 - Email and Social Media Investigation
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.content:
Chapter 1: E-Mail and Social Media Investigation
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 (CDS-361)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: forensics email social-media investigation

1.1 Role of Email Investigation
E-mail remains a primary medium for corporate and personal communication, making it a frequent source of evidence in Cybercrime cases such as phishing, harassment, industrial espionage, and financial fraud.
Key Goals:

Attribution: Identifying the sender (Authorship Analysis).
Traceability: Tracking the path of the email from source to destination.
Intent: Analyzing the content for motive or proof of conspiracy.

Client vs. Server Roles

Email Client (MUA - Mail User Agent): The specialized application used to send/receive mail (e.g., Outlook, Thunderbird). Stores local copies of emails (PST/OST files, mbox).
Email Server (MTA - Mail Transfer Agent): Handles the routing and delivery (e.g., Microsoft Exchange, Postfix). Stores logs of transactions, which are critical for proving an email was sent/received even if the client deleted it.


1.2 Examining Email Messages
Standard procedure allows investigators to recover deleted emails, analyze headers, and extract attachments.
1.2.1 Email Headers
The header is the most critical part of an email for forensics. It contains the metadata of the transmission.
Key Fields:

Return-Path: The address for bounce messages.
Received: The most important field. Read from Bottom to Top.

Bottom-most Received header usually indicates the originating IP/server.
Shows the chain of custody across MTAs.


Message-ID: A unique string assigned by the originating mail server (e.g., <abc.123@mail.google.com>).
X-Headers: Custom headers added by spam filters or clients (e.g., X-Originating-IP).

1.2.2 Email Authentication Protocols
Modern forensics relies on these to verify if an email is spoofed.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework): Checks if the sending IP is authorized by the domain’s DNS.

Result: Pass (Legit) / Fail (Spoofed).


DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): Cryptographic signature verifying the email body/headers haven’t been altered in transit.
DMARC: Uses SPF and DKIM to determine the policy for unauthenticated emails (Reject/Quarantine).


1.3 Tracing an E-mail Message

Extract the Originating IP: Look for the first Received header or X-Originating-IP.
Geolocation: Use Whois or IP Geolocation tools to resolve the IP to a physical location/ISP.
Time Zone Analysis: Correlate timestamps (UTC vs Local) to place the suspect at the scene.


1.4 Email Server Logs
When client-side evidence is destroyed, server logs are the fallback.

Microsoft Exchange Logs:

Transaction Logs (.log): Records all database changes.
SMTP Logs: Records protocol-level conversations (HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO).


Unix/Linux Logs:

/var/log/maillog or /var/log/mail.log.
Records Postfix/Sendmail activity including Message codes and delivery status.




1.5 Social Media Investigation
Social media forensics often overlaps with Mobile Forensics as most usage is mobile-based.
1.5.1 Challenges

Volatile Data: Stories/Status updates disappear after 24 hours.
Cloud Storage: Data typically resides on the provider’s server (Facebook/Instagram), not just the device.
Encryption: WhatsApp/Signal use End-to-End Encryption (E2EE), making interception impossible; data must be extracted from the endpoint (device).

1.5.2 Forensics Tools (2024/2025)

Magnet AXIOM: Excellent for recovering artifacts from cloud services and correlating them with mobile data.
Cellebrite UFED: The industry standard for physical extraction from mobile devices. Can bypass locks on many Android/iOS devices.
Oxygen Forensic Detective: Strong cloud extraction capabilities (Cloud Key extraction).
X1 Social Discovery: Specialized for crawling public social media profiles and preserving posts for court.

1.5.3 Mobile Social Media Forensics

Artifacts: Cache files, thumbnails, SQLite databases (msgstore.db for WhatsApp).
Techniques:

Logical Extraction: Getting accessible files (API-based).
Physical Extraction: Bit-by-bit copy of flash memory (Required for deleted messages).




Slip Questions & Answers
Q: How to extract email header in Gmail?
Open email → three-dot menu → Show original → Download Original. This gives you the full raw header.
Q: Identify sender, recipient, date, and servers from header

Sender: From: field
Recipient: To: field
Date/Time: Date: field
Servers: Each Received: line — read bottom to top; bottom = origin

Q: What time zone does sender’s computer reside in?
Look at Date: header from originating server. Offset like -0530 = IST (UTC+5:30).
Q: What time zone does sender’s mail server reside in?
Look at timestamp offset in bottom-most Received: header.
Q: Which IP to trace if email is spoofed?
Bottom-most Received: header IP — that’s the actual sending server. Run Whois/Geolocation on it.
Q: What is SPF and what does it tell about sender legitimacy?
SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a DNS TXT record listing IPs authorized to send email for a domain.

spf=pass → IP is authorized → sender likely legitimate
spf=fail → IP not authorized → likely spoofed

Q: Find DKIM signature — which domain signed? Was it verified?
Look for DKIM-Signature: header. d= tag = signing domain. Authentication-Results: shows dkim=pass (verified) or dkim=fail.
Q: DMARC record — what policy for failed authentication?
DNS TXT at _dmarc.domain.com. Policy (p=) options:

none → monitor only
quarantine → send to spam
reject → block completely

Q: Analyze Base64 encoded email content
Look for Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="file.pdf" followed by alphanumeric block.
Decode: base64 -d encoded.txt > output.pdf
Q: Forensic examination of compromised email account

Pull full headers of suspicious emails — check originating IPs
Check login history (Gmail: “Last account activity”)
Check forwarding rules — attackers set silent forwards
Check OAuth apps with account access
Cross-ref IPs in headers with known login locations

Q: Use MXToolbox / EmailTrackerPro to track sender’s IP

Copy full raw header
Paste into MXToolbox → Email Header Analyzer
Tool resolves each Received: hop, geolocates IPs, flags SPF/DKIM/DMARC status

Q: Steps to extract data from social media application

Identify platform (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp)
Logical extraction via ADB → pull SQLite DBs from device
WhatsApp: msgstore.db needs encryption key from /data/data/com.whatsapp/files/key
Cloud extraction via Magnet AXIOM (with credentials) or Cellebrite UFED Cloud
Public OSINT: X1 Social Discovery for public profiles

Q: Script to extract public profile from social media
import tweepy
client = tweepy.Client(bearer_token="YOUR_TOKEN")
user = client.get_user(username="target_handle",
                       user_fields=["name", "description", "location"])
print(user.data)
API endpoints: GET /2/users/by/username/:username (Twitter/X v2 API)

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.title: Chapter 2 - Mobile Device Forensics
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.content:
Chapter 2: Mobile Device Forensics
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 (CDS-361)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: forensics mobile android evidence-acquisition

2.1 Need and Challenges (2024)
Mobile devices are the central repository of personal data (Location, Chat, Health). However, forensics is increasingly difficult due to:

Encryption: Modern Android uses File-Based Encryption (FBE). Data cannot be accessed without the passcode or high-level exploits (e.g., GrayKey, Cellebrite Premium).
OS Fragmentation: Thousands of device models with customized OS versions (MIUI, OneUI) require specific bootloaders/exploits.
Anti-Forensics: Features like “Auto Factory Reset” after wrong attempts and Secure Folder/Second Space.


2.2 Mobile Architecture & File System
Android is built on the Linux Kernel.
Key Partitions

/system: Read-only partition containing the OS and pre-installed apps. Forensically less interesting unless looking for malware persistence.
/data: The Gold Mine. Contains specific user data:

/data/data/: App directories (Databases, Shared Preferences).
/data/misc/: WiFi keys, VPN configs.


/cache: Temporary files, OTA updates, and recovery logs.

File Systems

ext4: Standard Linux file system. Supports “Journaling” (helps recover some data).
F2FS (Flash-Friendly File System): Optimized for flash storage, widely used by Samsung. Harder to carve deleted data from than ext4.


2.3 Acquisition Processes
There are three main levels of data extraction:
2.3.1 Manual Acquisition

Method: Manually browsing the phone and taking photos/screenshots of the evidence.
Use Case: When the device cannot be connected to a PC (e.g., damaged port) or strict privacy laws prevent full imaging.
Pros: Simple, visual.
Cons: Misses hidden/deleted data; difficult to search.

2.3.2 Logical Acquisition (ADB)

Method: Extracts data accessible to the user via API (Standard Backup).
Tool: ADB (Android Debug Bridge).

Command: adb backup -apk -shared -all -f backup.ab.


Use Case: Unrooted phones where physical extraction isn’t possible.
Pros: Fast, universally supported.
Cons: Cannot access protected app data (e.g., WhatsApp DBs) if the app disallows backup.

2.3.3 Physical Acquisition

Method: Bit-by-bit copy of the flash memory (NAND). Creates a dd image (e.g., mmcblk0).
Requirement: Usually requires Root Access or a Bootloader Exploit (EDL Mode).
Techniques:

JTAG/ISP: Connect directly to motherboard test points (Hardware intensive).
Chip-Off: Desoldering the storage chip (Destructive, last resort).


Pros: Recovers Deleted Data from unallocated space.
Cons: Risk of bricking the device; expensive equipment.


2.4 Android Data Analysis
Once extracted (usually logically via ADB/Agent or Physically via Image), analysis involves parsing databases.
Key Artifact locations:

SMS/MMS: /data/data/com.android.providers.telephony/databases/mmssms.db
Contacts: /data/data/com.android.providers.contacts/databases/contacts2.db
Call Logs: /data/data/com.android.providers.contacts/databases/calllog.db
WhatsApp: /data/data/com.whatsapp/databases/msgstore.db (Encrypted, needs key).

Tools

Autopsy: Best open-source tool. Can parse Android Backup (.ab) and Raw Images.
Cellebrite UFED Physical Analyzer: The industry leader for decoding complex apps.
SQLite Browser: Essential for manually inspecting .db files extracted from the phone.

Deleted Data Recovery

File Carving: Searching the “Unallocated Space” of a physical image for headers/footers (e.g., looking for FF D8 ... FF D9 for JPEGs).
SQLite Wal/Journal: Uncommited transactions in Main Database files often contain “deleted” records that haven’t been overwritten yet.


Slip Questions & Answers
Q: Extract device information using ADB — create a report
adb devices                                    # verify device connected
adb shell getprop ro.product.manufacturer      # manufacturer
adb shell getprop ro.product.model             # model
adb shell getprop ro.build.version.release     # Android version
adb shell getprop ro.serialno                  # serial number
adb shell getprop ro.product.cpu.abi           # architecture
adb shell df -h                                # storage info
Report includes: device ID, model, OS version, storage, connected timestamp.
Q: What ADB command retrieves list of installed applications?
adb shell pm list packages          # all packages
adb shell pm list packages -3       # third-party only
adb shell pm list packages -s       # system apps only
Q: Which tool/method to create image of phone data, and why?

Logical (ADB backup): adb backup -apk -shared -all -f backup.ab — fast, no root, but misses deleted data
Physical (dd via ADB root shell): adb shell dd if=/dev/block/mmcblk0 | dd of=android.img — full bit-for-bit, recovers deleted data, needs root
Autopsy: Load .ab or raw image → automated artifact parsing
Why physical preferred: Only method that recovers deleted data from unallocated space

Q: How to use Autopsy to analyze Android image? File recovery options?

Open Autopsy → New Case → Add Data Source → select image file
Select ingest modules: Android Analyzer, File Type Identification, Keyword Search
Autopsy parses: SMS (mmssms.db), Contacts (contacts2.db), Call logs, Browser history
File Recovery options:

Data Artifacts → shows parsed app data
Deleted Files → lists carved deleted files from unallocated space
File Type → filter by images/video/audio
Right-click any file → Extract



Q: Extract list of image, video, audio files from mobile image
In Autopsy: Views → File Types → Images / Videos / Audio
Or via ADB:
adb shell find /sdcard -name "*.jpg" -o -name "*.mp4" -o -name "*.mp3"
Q: Retrieve metadata (date created, location) for files
# Install exiftool on host, pull file via ADB first
adb pull /sdcard/DCIM/Camera/photo.jpg
exiftool photo.jpg
# Shows: GPS coords, timestamp, camera model, software
Q: Extract and analyze call logs from mobile image

DB path: /data/data/com.android.providers.contacts/databases/calllog.db
Open with SQLite Browser → table calls → columns: number, date, duration, type (1=incoming, 2=outgoing, 3=missed)
In Autopsy: Data Artifacts → Call Logs

Q: Recover deleted data from mobile image

Physical image required (logical won’t have unallocated space)
File Carving: Autopsy or Foremost scans for JPEG FF D8, PNG 89 50 4E 47 etc.
SQLite WAL: Check -wal and -journal files alongside .db files — contain uncommitted (deleted) rows
Autopsy: Deleted Files view shows recovered entries

Q: Recover deleted SMS messages — tools + integrity verification
Tools: Autopsy, Cellebrite UFED Physical Analyzer, SQLite Browser
Steps:

Extract mmssms.db + mmssms.db-wal / mmssms.db-journal
Open in SQLite Browser → check sms table — deleted rows may still be in WAL
Hash the DB before and after (md5sum mmssms.db) to prove integrity
In Autopsy: Data Artifacts → Messages

Q: What permissions required for ADB system-level access?

USB Debugging must be enabled (Developer Options)
For /data access: Root required (or bootloader unlock + custom recovery)
Physical acquisition (dd of full partition): Root shell via adb root
No special OS permissions needed for logical backup on user partition

Q: Security risks of enabling ADB

Full shell access to device over USB
Silent app install/uninstall (adb install malicious.apk)
Data exfiltration (adb pull)
Credential theft if connected to untrusted computer
Bypass screen lock on some older Android versions
Mitigation: Disable after use, always authorize only known computers

Q: Recover contacts via Google account — steps + limitations
Steps:

Go to contacts.google.com → Settings → Undo changes
Select restore point (up to 30 days back) → Restore
Alternative: Google Account → Data & Privacy → Google Takeout → export Contacts

Limitations:

30-day window only
Only synced contacts recoverable — locally stored contacts lost
Contacts deleted before sync-to-Google are unrecoverable this way
No fine-grained per-contact restore — full rollback only

Q: Security/privacy concerns when recovering deleted mobile data

Recovered data may contain third-party private info (other people’s messages)
Legal authorization (warrant/consent) required before extraction
Chain of custody must be maintained — hash image before and after
Sensitive data (banking, health) must be handled per IT Act / PDPB compliance
Risk of re-victimization if victim’s intimate data is exposed during investigation

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.title: Chapter 3 - Multimedia Forensics
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.content:
Chapter 3: Multimedia Forensics
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 (CDS-361)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: forensics multimedia steganography data-recovery

3.1 Graphics File Formats
Understanding file types is critical for identifying the origin of an image.
3.1.1 Bitmap (Raster) Images

Definition: Made up of a grid of individual pixels. Resolution dependent.
Formats: JPEG, PNG, BMP, GIF, TIFF.
Forensic Value:

EXIF Metadata: Heavily present in JPEGs from cameras/phones. Contains Model, GPS, Timestamp, and Software used.
Compression Artifacts: JPEG uses “Lossy” compression. Repeated saving degrades quality, leaving a history of edits.



3.1.2 Vector Graphics

Definition: Defined by mathematical formulas (lines, curves). Scalable without quality loss.
Formats: SVG, AI, EPS.
Forensic Value: Metadata inside XML structures (like in SVG) can reveal authorship.

3.1.3 Metafile Graphics

Definition: Hybrid format containing both Bitmap and Vector data.
Formats: WMF (Windows Metafile), EMF.


3.2 Data Compression

Lossless (PNG, TIFF, BMP): Retains every bit of data. Best for hiding data using Steganography.
Lossy (JPEG): Discards “unnecessary” data to save space. Makes recovering hidden messages harder but leaves quantization artifacts useful for detecting tampering.


3.3 Data Carving (Recovering Deleted Files)
When a file is deleted, the OS removes the pointer, but the data remains in Unallocated Space until overwritten. “Carving” extracts this data.
Technique: Header/Footer Carving
Forensic tools scan the raw disk bytes for specific signatures.

JPEG: Starts with FF D8, ends with FF D9.
PNG: Starts with 89 50 4E 47.

Tools:

Foremost: Linux CLI tool. Fast header/footer carving.
Scalpel: Configurable, high-performance carver.
PhotoRec: Specialized in recovering multimedia from damaged SD cards/disks.


3.4 Steganography & Steganalysis

Steganography: Hiding a secret message inside a cover file (e.g., changing the Least Significant Bit (LSB) of pixel colors).
Steganalysis: The art of detecting hidden messages.

Detection Tools (2024)

Stegdetect: Automated tool for detecting JPHide, JSteg, OutGuess.
StegExpose: Java-based tool for LSB steganalysis.
StegSpy: Identifies the signature of the program used to hide the message.
Binwalk: Analyzes file headers to find hidden files appended to images.
ExifTool: Checks for anomalies in metadata where text might be hidden.


3.5 Copyright Issues
Forensics is often used to prove IP theft.

Hash Analysis: Comparing the MD5/SHA1 hash of a seized image against the original.
Thumbnail Cache: Checking thumbs.db (Windows) can prove a suspect viewed/had the image even if the main file is deleted.


Slip Questions & Answers
Q: Extract and analyze metadata from images/videos in mobile image
# Pull files from mobile first
adb pull /sdcard/DCIM/Camera/ ./evidence_photos/
 
# Run exiftool on folder
exiftool -r ./evidence_photos/
 
# Key fields to check
exiftool photo.jpg | grep -E "GPS|Date|Make|Model|Software"
EXIF fields relevant to forensics:

GPS Latitude/Longitude → physical location when photo taken
Date/Time Original → actual capture time (not file system time)
Make / Model → device that captured the image
Software → editing software (proves manipulation if Photoshop shows up on a “camera” photo)

Q: How to retrieve metadata for image, video, audio files (date created, location)

Images (JPEG/PNG): ExifTool → exiftool filename.jpg
Videos (MP4): ExifTool or MediaInfo → shows creation time, GPS, encoder, duration
Audio (MP3): ExifTool → ID3 tags — artist, recorder device, creation date
In Autopsy: File → right-click → File Metadata — shows EXIF inline

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.title: Chapter 4 - Cloud Forensics
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.content:
Chapter 4: Cloud Forensics
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 (CDS-361)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: forensics cloud AWS Azure investigation

4.1 Cloud Computing Overview
Cloud forensics differs from traditional forensics because the evidence is stored on remote, third-party servers.
4.1.1 Service Models & Forensics

SaaS (Software as a Service - Gmail, Dropbox):

Forensics is limited to Logs provided by the CSP. Use API-based extraction.


PaaS (Platform as a Service - Google App Engine):

Access to Application logs and some configuration data.


IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service - AWS EC2):

Highest control. Investigators can take Snapshots of the Virtual Machine (VM) disk and analyze it like a physical hard drive.




4.2 Challenges in Cloud Forensics
4.2.1 Technical Challenges

No Physical Access: Investigators cannot seize the server rack. Reliance on “Remote Forensics”.
Multi-tenancy: Your suspect’s data resides on the same physical disk as 100 other companies. You cannot image the whole disk without violating others’ privacy.
Volatility: Cloud resources (Containers/Lambda functions) can spin up and vanish in seconds.

4.2.2 Legal Challenges

Jurisdiction: A crime in India might use data stored on a server in Ireland owned by a US company. Which law applies?
SLA (Service Level Agreement): Contracts often limit what data the CSP must provide to the customer during an incident.


4.3 Shared Responsibility Model
Crucial for determining WHO investigates what.

CSP (Provider - AWS/Azure): Responsible for Security OF the Cloud (Hardware, Global Network, Hypervisor).
Customer: Responsible for Security IN the Cloud (User Data, IAM Permissions, OS patching in IaaS).


4.4 Conducting an Investigation
4.4.1 Client-Side Evidence (On PC)
Even without cloud access, the suspect’s laptop holds clues.

Prefetch Files: Provide proof that a cloud app (e.g., dropbox.exe) was executed.
Browser Artifacts: URLs visited, Cached tokens.
Sync Folders: Local copies of cloud files (e.g., C:\Users\User\OneDrive).

4.4.2 Analysis Tools (2024)

Native Tools:

AWS CloudTrail: Logs every API call (Who did what).
Azure Monitor: Track activity logs.


Forensic Suites:

Magnet AXIOM Cloud: Extracts data from Google/O365 using admin credentials.
Cellebrite UFED Cloud: Accesses cloud backups of mobile devices.



4.4.3 Anti-Forensics
Suspects may use “Time-stomping” on cloud metadata or encrypted containers (Veracrypt) stored on the cloud to hide evidence.

Slip Questions & Answers
Q: Use WinHex to find last access time of Google Drive on computer

Open WinHex → Tools → Open Disk → select suspect drive
Navigate to C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\Google\Drive\
Select any file → Properties panel shows MAC timestamps (Modified, Accessed, Created)
For precise NTFS timestamps: Tools → Open Disk → Navigate to $MFT → search for Drive-related entries
$MFT stores 100-nanosecond precision timestamps for every file

Q: Determine how many times Google Drive was accessed on system

Registry: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\UserAssist → tracks GUI app execution count (encoded in ROT13)
Prefetch: C:\Windows\Prefetch\GOOGLEDRIVESYNC.EXE-XXXXX.pf → stores run count + last 8 run timestamps
Event Logs: Windows Security log, Event ID 4688 (process creation) → filter for googledrivesync.exe
LNK files: C:\Users\[user]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Recent\ — Jump Lists show recent Drive file accesses

Q: What artifacts created on computer when Google Drive is used?








































ArtifactLocationEvidence ValueSync folderC:\Users\[user]\Google Drive\Local copies of cloud filesSQLite config DBAppData\Local\Google\Drive\user_default\sync_config.dbTracks synced file names + IDsPrefetch fileC:\Windows\Prefetch\GOOGLEDRIVESYNC.EXE-*.pfProof of execution + timestampsRegistry keyHKCU\Software\Google\DriveLast run, account emailBrowser cacheChrome profile cacheWeb interface usage historyThumbnail cachethumbs.db / Windows thumbnail cacheProves files were viewed

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.title: Chapter 5 - Virtual Machine and Network Forensics
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Notes/Chapte.content:
Chapter 5: Virtual Machine and Network Forensics
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 (CDS-361)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: forensics virtualization network ram-capture

5.1 Virtual Machine Forensics
Virtualization allows multiple Operating Systems (Guests) to run on a single Host.
5.1.1 Hypervisor Types

Type 1 (Bare-Metal):

Runs directly on hardware (e.g., VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V).
Investigation: Difficult. Requires accessing the hypervisor logs or management console (vSphere) to snapshot VMs.


Type 2 (Hosted):

Runs as an app on an OS (e.g., VirtualBox, VMware Workstation).
Investigation: Easier. The VM is just a file on the Host OS (e.g., .vmdk or .vdi files in C:\Users\Documents\).



5.1.2 Examination

Snapshots: Preserve the state of a VM at a specific time. Extremely valuable for seeing “history”.
Mounting Images: Forensic tools can mount .vmdk files as if they were physical disks.


5.2 Live Acquisition (RAM Capture)
Capturing volatile memory (RAM) from a running system before pulling the plug.
Why? RAM contains:

Decrypted passwords/keys.
Running processes (Malware often lives only in RAM).
Unsaved documents.

Process

Preparation: Use a sanitized USB drive containing the forensic tools (Evidence Collection). Do NOT install tools on the suspect machine.
Capture: Run the tool with Admin privileges.
Output: Saves a .mem or .raw file to the USB drive.

Tools (2024)

FTK Imager: Can capture RAM (“Capture Memory”) to a raw file.
DumpIt: Simple command-line tool. Fast.
Magnet RAM Capture: Free tool by Magnet Forensics.


5.3 Network Forensics
The monitoring and analysis of computer network traffic for the purposes of information gathering, legal evidence, or intrusion detection.
5.3.1 Network Traffic Acquisition

Full Packet Capture (PCAP): Recording every packet. Resource intensive but provides the best evidence.
Log Analysis: Analyzing Firewall, IDS, or Router logs (NetFlow).

5.3.2 Tools

Wireshark: The industry standard for analyzing .pcap files. Allows deep inspection of packet headers (TCP/IP handshake) and payloads.
Tcpdump: CLI packet analyzer.
Network Miner: Passive network sniffer that extracts files (images, certs) from traffic.

5.3.3 Honeynets
A network set up with intentional vulnerabilities (Honeypots) to invite attacks.

Purpose: To study attacker behavior, tools, and Zero-day exploits in a controlled environment.
Forensic Value: Any traffic found on a Honeynet is suspicious by definition.


Slip Questions & Answers
Q: Wireshark — top 10 websites visited / accessed from VM

Open Wireshark → capture on relevant interface (or load .pcap)
Statistics → Endpoints → IPv4 tab → sort by Packets (descending)
Or: Statistics → Protocol Hierarchy → drill into HTTP/DNS
For DNS-based resolution: Statistics → DNS → sort by queries
Filter display: dns to see all domain lookups → export as CSV

Q: Indicators of data exfiltration, unauthorized access, malware comms

Exfiltration: Large outbound transfers to unknown IPs; unusual protocols (DNS tunneling on port 53, ICMP payload)
Unauthorized access: SSH/RDP from unexpected source IPs; failed auth bursts (brute force)
Malware C2: Periodic beaconing at fixed intervals; connections to uncommon ports (4444, 1337); JA3 fingerprint mismatches
Wireshark filter: ip.dst != [known_internal_range] to isolate suspicious outbound

Q: How to use tcpdump to examine / capture network traffic
# Basic capture
tcpdump -i eth0
 
# Save to file
tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap
 
# Read saved file
tcpdump -r capture.pcap
 
# Filter by port (SMTP)
tcpdump -i eth0 port 25
 
# Filter by host
tcpdump -i eth0 host 192.168.1.100
 
# Verbose + no DNS resolution (faster)
tcpdump -i eth0 -nn -vv
 
# Detect SYN scans
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'
 
# Suspicious reverse shell port
tcpdump -i eth0 port 4444
Q: Filter packets to find suspicious activity in VM
# Outbound to non-RFC1918 IPs only
tcpdump -i eth0 'not (dst net 192.168.0.0/16 or dst net 10.0.0.0/8)'
 
# Large packets (potential exfil)
tcpdump -i eth0 'len > 1400'
In Wireshark:
ip.dst != 192.168.0.0/16 && ip.dst != 10.0.0.0/8   # external only
tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0             # SYN scan
http.request.method == "POST"                         # data submission

Q: Investigate email logs on mail server using forensic tools

Linux: /var/log/maillog or /var/log/mail.log (Postfix/Sendmail)
Exchange: C:\Program Files\Microsoft\Exchange Server\V15\TransportRoles\Logs\
Look for: MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, HELO/EHLO, delivery status codes (250=OK, 550=rejected)
Tools: grep, awk, Splunk, or import into Wireshark if SMTP over network

Q: Wireshark — capture and analyze SMTP traffic
Filter: tcp.port == 25  (or port 587 for submission)

Right-click packet → Follow TCP Stream → see full SMTP conversation:

EHLO = client greeting
MAIL FROM: = sender
RCPT TO: = recipient
DATA = email content (headers + body)
250 OK = accepted

Q: Extract and decode MIME-encoded email messages

In Wireshark: Follow TCP Stream of SMTP session → copy DATA section
Identify Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64 sections
Decode: echo "base64string" | base64 -d > attachment.pdf
MIME boundary separates parts — look for --boundary_string

Q: IDS (Snort) to monitor traffic from VM
# Run Snort on VM's NIC
snort -i eth0 -c /etc/snort/snort.conf -A console
 
# Alert mode — log to file
snort -i eth0 -c /etc/snort/snort.conf -l /var/log/snort/
Rules fire on signatures (port scans, known exploits, C2 beacons).
Logs: /var/log/snort/alert
Q: Encrypted network traffic analysis in virtualized environment
Cannot decrypt without keys, but can analyze:

TLS SNI field (Server Name Indication) — reveals destination hostname even in encrypted traffic
Certificate metadata — issuer, validity, self-signed flag
Packet size + timing patterns — identify protocol fingerprints (JA3 hash)
Volume anomalies — sudden large encrypted transfers
For VMs: capture traffic at virtual switch level on host (pre-encryption if TLS terminated at load balancer)

Q: What info from VM log files in crime investigation?
VM logs reveal:

Power-on / power-off timestamps → places suspect at keyboard
Snapshot creation times → “frozen state” at time of incident
Network adapter changes → evidence of network isolation/pivot
USB device connections (via host logs)
Guest OS crashes or forced shutdowns

VMware .log example entries:
2025-01-15T10:23:01.456Z| vmx| Powering on VM
2025-01-15T14:45:22.123Z| vmx| Snapshot taken: 'Before_Attack'
2025-01-15T18:10:05.789Z| vmx| Powering off VM

Q: Investigate hypervisor logs for unauthorized access / VM timestamps

VMware Workstation: vmware.log in VM folder — power events, snapshot history
VirtualBox: VBox.log per-VM
Hyper-V: Windows Event Viewer → Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Worker and Hyper-V-VMMS
Look for: unexpected power-on times, snapshot creation, config changes

Q: Extract VM log files, config files, snapshots for forensic analysis

Config: .vmx (VMware) or .vbox (VirtualBox) — contains MAC, RAM, OS, shared folders
Disk image: .vmdk / .vdi — mount with FTK Imager or Autopsy as physical disk
Snapshots: .vmsd (snapshot tree metadata) + .vmsn (snapshot state)
Process: Copy entire VM folder to forensic workstation → hash everything first

Q: Forensic artifacts in VM vs physical machine





























VM-SpecificPhysical OnlySnapshot files (time-travel)SMART data (disk health/wear).vmdk / .vdi as host filesPhysical port connectionsVirtual NIC (host can capture all traffic)Hardware serial numbersHost/Guest shared folder artifactsRAM soldered to board (harder to capture)Hypervisor management logs
Q: Acquire forensic image of host running multiple VMs

Do NOT shutdown — capture RAM first (FTK Imager “Capture Memory”)
Image the host disk with FTK Imager / dd → captures all VM files (.vmdk, .log, .vmx)
Each .vmdk file = one VM disk — load individually in Autopsy
Preserve snapshot files — they contain historical states
Hash everything: md5sum host_image.dd

Q: Network logs to trace host↔VM activity + VM creation/deletion via system logs
Log types:

Firewall logs: traffic between host and VMs (NAT/bridge)
IDS/IPS logs: alerts triggered by VM traffic
Hypervisor event logs: VM lifecycle events
OS System logs: Event ID 13002 (Hyper-V VM start), 13003 (stop)

Determine VM created/modified/deleted:

Windows: Event Viewer → System → filter by Hyper-V source
VMware: vmware.log timestamp of first entry = creation; config .vmx createDate field
VirtualBox: VirtualBox.xml in ~/.VirtualBox/ tracks all registered VMs with creation time

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Practicals/P.title: Practical 1 Notes - Email Forensics
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Practicals/P.content:
Practical 1 Notes: Email Forensics
Overview
Email forensics involves analyzing email headers and content to investigate potential cybercrimes, phishing attempts, or unauthorized communications. The “header” of an email contains crucial metadata that tells the story of the email’s journey.
Key Concepts
1. Email Headers
The header is a section of code that contains information about the sender, recipient, and the path the email took to get to your inbox.

Return-Path: The email address where bounce messages are sent.
Received: The most important field. Read from bottom to top.

The bottom-most Received header is the originating server (first hop).
The top-most Received header is the receiving server (last hop, your provider).


Message-ID: A unique identifier for the email.
Authentication Results: Critical security checks to verify the sender’s identity.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework): Specifies which IP addresses are authorized to send email for a domain. Check for spf=pass.
DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): Adds a digital signature to the email header to prove it hasn’t been altered. Check for dkim=pass.
DMARC: A policy that tells the receiving server how to handle emails that fail SPF or DKIM checks.



2. Identifying the Sender (True Source)
Spoofing allows an attacker to fake the “From” address. To find the real sender:

Look for the first (bottom-most) Received header.
It will often show the IP address of the sending device or server.
SPF (Sender Policy Framework): A security mechanism where a domain lists the IPs allowed to send email on its behalf.

Pass: The IP is authorized.
Fail/Softfail: The IP might be spoofed.



3. Attachments & Encoding
Email protocols (SMTP) were originally designed for text only. To send files (images, documents), they are encoded into text formats.

MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions): The standard for formatting non-ASCII messages.
Base64: A common encoding scheme. If you see a block of random-looking alphanumeric characters in the raw source, it’s likely a Base64 encoded attachment.

Structure: Often starts with Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="example.pdf".



4. Time Zones
Headers include timestamps for each hop.

Format: Date: Mon, 29 Dec 2025 10:55:00 -0800 (PST)
-0800: Indicates the time zone offset from UTC (Coordinated Universal Time).
By looking at the offset in the Date header from the SOURCE (sender), you can infer their general geographic region (or at least their system’s configuration).

Analysis Checklist

Download Original: Always work with the full raw header/source (in Gmail: “Show original”).
Trace path: Follow the Received headers from bottom to top.
Check IP: Take the originating IP and look it up on a “Whois” or “IP Geolocation” service.
Verify Auth: Look for spf=pass and dkim=pass.

Tools

Manual Inspection: Reading headers directly.
MxToolbox: Online tool to parse headers.
Google Admin Toolbox Messageheader: Visualizes the path.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Slip-Revisio.title: Slip Revision Master
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Slip-Revisio.content:
DF 2 — Slip Revision Master
Subject: Digital Forensics II (CDS-361 / Lab CDS-364)
Tags: forensics exam slip-revision df2
Last refreshed: 2026-04-12

Slip Format

3 Hours | 35 Marks

Q1 [15M] — Practical task
Q2 [15M] — Practical task

Q2: Use WinHex to find last access time of Google Drive on computer
How to solve (5 steps):

Navigate to C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\Google\Drive\

Executive Summary
Case Information (case#, investigator, date)

Conclusion

Q1: What info from VM log files in crime investigation?
VM logs reveal:

Power-on/off timestamps → places suspect at keyboard
Snapshot creation times → “frozen state” at incident
Network adapter changes → evidence of pivot/isolation
USB connections (via host logs)
Guest OS crashes or forced shutdowns

VMware .log example:
2025-01-15T10:23:01Z | vmx | Powering on VM
2025-01-15T14:45:22Z | vmx | Snapshot: 'Before_Attack'
2025-01-15T18:10:05Z | vmx | Powering off VM

Memory trick: “PSN-U” — Power events, Snapshots, Network changes, USB
→ Full answer: Q What info from VM log files in crime investigation

Q2: SPF record — what does it tell? + Find DKIM signature
SPF:

DNS TXT record listing IPs authorized to send for a domain
spf=pass → IP authorized → likely legit
spf=fail → IP NOT authorized → likely spoofed

DKIM:

Look for DKIM-Signature: header
d= tag = signing domain
Authentication-Results: shows dkim=pass or dkim=fail

Memory trick: “SPF = Sender Police, DKIM = Digital Ink”
→ Full answers: Q What is SPF and what does it tell about sender legitimacy | Q Find DKIM signature which domain signed Was it verified

Q1: tcpdump — capture and filter suspicious activity
# Outbound to non-internal IPs only (detect exfil)
tcpdump -i eth0 'not (dst net 192.168.0.0/16 or dst net 10.0.0.0/8)'
 
# Large packets = potential data exfiltration
tcpdump -i eth0 'len > 1400'
 
# Detect SYN scans
tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'
 
# Suspicious reverse shell
tcpdump -i eth0 port 4444
Wireshark equivalents:
ip.dst != 192.168.0.0/16     # external traffic
tcp.flags.syn == 1            # SYN scan
http.request.method == "POST" # data submission

Memory trick: “ELS” — External traffic, Large packets, SYN scans
→ Full answer: Q Filter packets to find suspicious activity in VM

Q2: Email logs on mail server + Wireshark SMTP + decode MIME
Email logs:

Linux: /var/log/maillog or /var/log/mail.log
Look for: MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, HELO/EHLO, status codes

Wireshark SMTP:
Filter: tcp.port == 25

Right-click → Follow TCP Stream → see full conversation
MIME decode:

Follow TCP Stream → copy DATA section
Find Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
echo "base64string" | base64 -d > attachment.pdf

Memory trick: “MIME = base64 in disguise”
→ Full answers: Q Investigate email logs on mail server | Q Extract and decode MIME-encoded email messages

Q1: Write script to collect social media profile data + API endpoints
How to solve:
import requests
 
# Twitter/X API v2 example
headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_TOKEN"}
url = "api.twitter.com/2/users/by/username/targetuser"
params = {"user.fields": "created_at,description,public_metrics"}
 
response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params)
data = response.json()
print(data)
Key API endpoints (for exam):

Twitter/X: /2/users/by/username/{username}
Facebook Graph: /v18.0/{user-id}?fields=name,email
LinkedIn: /v2/me (OAuth2 required)

Evidence to collect: username, bio, follower count, creation date, linked accounts
Memory trick: “BFCL” — Bearer token, Fields param, Check creation date, Link accounts
→ Full answer: Q Write script to extract social media profile data using API

Q2: Wireshark — live capture + extract credentials from HTTP
How to solve:

Start capture: Wireshark → select interface → Start
Filter for login traffic: http.request.method == "POST"
Follow TCP stream → look for username= or password= in form data
For FTP: filter ftp → credentials sent in plain text
For Telnet: filter telnet → entire session unencrypted

Wireshark filters:
http.request.method == "POST"    # form submissions
ftp.request.command == "PASS"    # FTP passwords
telnet                            # full telnet stream

Memory trick: “PFT plain text trio” — POST forms, FTP, Telnet = always plaintext
Mark booster: Note HTTPS/TLS traffic cannot be decoded without private key — shows examiner you know the limit
→ Full answer: Q Use Wireshark to capture live traffic and identify credentials

Slip 13 — IDS Snort for VM + Android Image Creation
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 | Tags: slip network mobile

Q1: IDS Snort on VM + analyze encrypted traffic
Snort on VM:
snort -i eth0 -c /etc/snort/snort.conf -A full    # live mode
snort -r capture.pcap -c /etc/snort/snort.conf    # read pcap
Snort rule syntax:
alert tcp any any -> 192.168.1.0/24 4444 (msg:"Reverse Shell Detected"; sid:1001;)

action protocol src_ip src_port -> dst_ip dst_port (options)
Encrypted traffic analysis:

Cannot decrypt TLS without private key
But can analyze: JA3 fingerprint (TLS client hello) → identify malware by TLS pattern
Check: certificate issuer, SNI field, connection frequency
Wireshark: ssl.handshake.type == 1 → Client Hello

Memory trick: “JA3 = TLS fingerprint” — even HTTPS leaks identity via handshake pattern
Mark booster: Mention Zeek/Bro alongside Snort for passive network monitoring in VMs
→ Full answer: Q Configure Snort IDS on VM and analyze encrypted traffic

Q2: Create forensic image of Android + analyze it
How to solve:

Physical image (rooted): adb shell dd if=/dev/block/mmcblk0 | dd of=android.img
Logical backup: adb backup -apk -shared -all -f backup.ab
Convert backup: dd if=backup.ab bs=24 skip=1 | python3 -c "import zlib,sys; sys.stdout.buffer.write(zlib.decompress(sys.stdin.buffer.read()))" > backup.tar
Analyze in Autopsy: Add Data Source → select android.img → run ingest modules

Key artifacts:

/data/data/ — app private data
/sdcard/ — user media
/data/misc/wifi/wpa_supplicant.conf — saved WiFi passwords

Memory trick: “DSD” — DD image, Shared backup, Data/data artifacts
→ Full answer: Q Create forensic image of Android device and analyze artifacts

Slip 14 — MXToolbox SPF/DKIM/DMARC + Multiple VMs Image
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 | Tags: slip email vm

Q1: Analyze email header + SPF/DKIM/DMARC
How to solve:

Open MXToolbox / Email Header Analyzer.
Paste raw email header into the tool.
Look for Authentication-Results: header row line.

What they do:

SPF: Checks if sender IP is authorized by domain owner.
DKIM: Cryptographic signature to ensure email wasn’t tampered with.
DMARC: Policy that tells receiver what to do (reject, quarantine) if SPF/DKIM fails.

Memory trick: “Sender Domain Policy” → SPF verifies sender IP, DKIM verifies domain integrity, DMARC enforces policy.
→ Full answer: Q What is SPF and what does it tell about sender legitimacy?

Q2: Forensic image of host with multiple VMs + Network logs
How to solve:

Acquisition: Image the host machine’s physical drive using FTK Imager or dd. This automatically captures all VM virtual disks (.vmdk, .vdi) inside it.
Analysis: Mount the host image in Autopsy, browse to the hypervisor directory (e.g., C:\Users\Public\Documents\Hyper-V), and extract the VM disks.

Network Logs to trace activity:

Firewall logs: Show connections between host IP and VM NAT IPs.
IDS/IPS (Snort): Detects malicious traffic crossing the virtual switch.
System Logs: Hypervisor logs (e.g., vmware.log) show VM startup, network interface bridging.

Memory trick: Image the host, extract the guest. Logs = FIS (Firewall, IDS, System).
→ Full answer: Q Acquire forensic image of host running multiple VMs

Slip 15 — VM Configs + Google Drive Access Count
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 | Tags: slip vm cloud

Q1: Extract VM log files, configs, snapshots + forensic artifacts vs physical
How to solve:

Locate the VM folder on the host (e.g., Documents\Virtual Machines).
Identify target files: .vmx (VMware Config), .vmem (RAM), .log (VMware logs), .vmsn (Snapshot).
Copy these files as evidence before booting anything.

How is VM different from Physical?

VMs have Snapshots (can recover system states fast).
VMs use Virtual Hardware (MAC addresses usually start with VMware/VBox OUIs, e.g., 00:50:56).
VMs have their own RAM files (.vmem) saved to disk.

Memory trick: “Config, Logs, Snap, RAM” = CLSR. VMs freeze time (snapshots) and fake hardware.
→ Full answer: Q Extract VM log files, config files, snapshots for forensic analysis

Q2: Determine number of times Google Drive accessed + artifacts created
How to solve:

Use WinHex or Autopsy to parse the Windows Registry.
Navigate to NTUSER.DAT (User Profile) → Software\Google\Drive.
Alternatively, check Google Drive’s local SQLite database (sync_config.db).

Artifacts created:

Prefetch files for googledrivesync.exe.
SQLite databases storing sync logs.
Local cache folder showing downloaded encrypted chunks.

Memory trick: Count the Prefetch executes and check the sync_config.db SQLite entries.
→ Full answer: Q Determine how many times Google Drive was accessed on system

Slip 16 — VM Logs Detect + WinHex Cloud Timestamp
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 | Tags: slip vm cloud

Q1: Extract VM logs to reconstruct activities + Network logs to trace interactions
How to solve:

Open vmware.log or VBox VBox.log via Event Viewer or directly in text editor.
Search for “PowerOn”, “Suspend”, “NIC connected” to reconstruct timeline.
Check Windows Event IDs (like 4624 for Logons) within the guest OS.

Network logs for interactions:

Map the VM’s NAT/Bridged virtual IP from firewall logs.
Match external traffic hitting the host’s virtual NIC wrapper.

Memory trick: Timeline is in .log. Interactions are in the virtual firewall.
→ Full answer:  VM timestamps

Q2: WinHex for Cloud Transaction History + Timestamps
How to solve:

Open the physical drive in WinHex.
Locate the localized cloud database (e.g., cloud_graph.db or Dropbox logs).
View Hex values to find Unix Epoch timestamps for “Created”, “Modified”, “Deleted”.

Forensic techniques:

Carving: If deleted, use file carving to recover the sync SQLite DB.
Translation: Convert Unix hex timestamps to human-readable using data interpreters.

Memory trick: Hex editors hunt the Epoch.
→ Full answer: 4.4 Conducting an Investigation

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Slips/Slip-1.content:
Slip 17 — Mobile Phishing + Local vs Cloud Modified Files
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 | Tags: slip mobile cloud

Q1: Extract email and SMS for phishing + Metadata identification
How to solve:

Email: Extract EML/MSG or SQLite DB (e.g., EmailProvider.db).
SMS: Pull /data/data/com.android.providers.telephony/databases/mmssms.db.
Identify via Metadata: Search for spoofed Sender IDs in SMS (address field) or malicious URLs in the email body.

How metadata helps:

Timestamp differences can reveal automated spam.
IP Headers/Routing shows the real country of origin.

Memory trick: SMS is mmssms.db. Email is EmailProvider.db. Metadata unmasks the spoof.
→ Full answer: Chapter 2 - Mobile Device Forensics

Q2: Differentiate locally modified vs directly in cloud
How to solve:

Locally modified: File’s MAC (Modified/Accessed/Created) timestamps in the local NTFS/FAT will differ from the sync timestamp. Sync agent logs will show an “Upload” event.
Directly in cloud: Sync agent logs will show a “Download” event. The local file creation date will match the cloud sync date, not original creation date.
Look for file versioning IDs inside the cloud provider’s SQLite logs.

Memory trick: Local = “Upload” event. Cloud = “Download” event.
→ Full answer: 4.4 Conducting an Investigation

Slip 18 — FTK Imager VM + WinHex Google Drive Registry
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 | Tags: slip vm cloud

Q1: Forensic image of host running VM (FTK Imager Lite)
How to solve:

Connect target host drive via write-blocker or run FTK Imager Lite on live system.
Select File > Create Disk Image → Choose Physical Drive.
Save as E01 (EnCase) format for verification (hash calculation).

Data collected:

Full host OS + allocated & unallocated space.
VM configuration files (.vmx).
VM virtual disks (.vmdk).
Network logs (Windows Event Logs → Security).

Memory trick: FTK grabs the whole pie (Host), which includes the slices (VMs).
→ Full answer: Q Acquire forensic image of host running multiple VMs

Q2: WinHex Windows Registry Google Drive Activity
How to solve:

Export NTUSER.DAT and open in WinHex or Registry Viewer.
Navigate to Software\Classes\Local Settings\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Shell\MuiCache and find Googledrivesync.exe to see last execution.
Check UserAssist keys to see how many times it was launched.

Memory trick: Registry MuiCache and UserAssist are the snitches for executed software.
→ Full answer: Q Use WinHex to find last access time of Google Drive on computer

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/DF-2/Slips/Slip-1.content:
Slip 19 — VM Snapshots Recover + Email Header Spoofing
Subject: Digital Forensics-2 | Tags: slip vm email

Q1: Extract and examine VM snapshots + Recover deleted files
How to solve:

Navigate to the VM datastore folder.
Locate the .vmsn (Memory state) and .vmdk snapshot differencing disks (e.g., vm-000001.vmdk).
To recover deleted files, attach the old snapshot .vmdk to a forensic analysis tool (like Autopsy or FTK Imager) as an image file.

Why this works:

Snapshots freeze the file system at a specific point in time before the file was deleted.

Memory trick: Snapshots are time machines. Mount the .vmsn/.vmdk to travel back.
→ Full answer: Q Extract VM log files, config files, snapshots for forensic analysis

Q2: Analyze email headers for origin + Identify spoofed senders
How to solve:

Open the raw email header.
Read from bottom to top (the bottom-most Received: header is the origin server).
Check the Authentication-Results: block (SPF, DKIM, DMARC will Fail if spoofed).

Identify malicious links:

Extract URLs from the body and check against threat intel (VirusTotal).
Look for mismatched display vs underlying URLs (e.g., <a href="evil.com">paypal.com</a>).

Memory trick: Bottom-up trace. Spoofers fail SPF.
→ Full answer: Q Which IP to trace if email is spoofed?

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.title: Chapter 1 - Introduction
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.content:
Chapter 1: Introduction to Malware
Subject: Malware Analysis (CDS-367A)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: malware virus worm trojan ransomware static-analysis dynamic-analysis

1.1 Malware Definition & Concepts
Malware (Malicious Software) is any software intentionally designed to cause disruption to a computer, server, client, or computer network, leak private information, gain unauthorized access to information or systems, deprive users of access to information, or which unknowingly interferes with the user’s computer security and privacy.
1.1.1 Malicious Actions
Malware is developed to perform various harmful activities:

Data Theft: Stealing sensitive data like passwords, credit card numbers (e.g., Spyware, Keyloggers).
Disruption: Causing system crashes or deleting files (e.g., Wipers, Viruses).
Extortion: Encrypting data and demanding ransom (e.g., Ransomware).
Resource Hijacking: Using the victim’s CPU for mining cryptocurrency or DDoS attacks (e.g., Cryptominers, Botnets).
Espionage: Monitoring user activity (e.g., Rootkits, Spyware).

1.1.2 Common Types of Malware

Virus: Requires a host program to attach itself to. Replicates when the host is executed.
Worm: Standalone program that replicates itself to spread to other computers (often via network) without human action.
Trojan Horse: Disguises itself as legitimate software (e.g., a game or update) to trick the user into installing it. Does not replicate.
Ransomware: Encrypts user files and demands payment for the decryption key (e.g., WannaCry).
Spyware/Adware: Collects data or displays unwanted ads.
Rootkit: Provides privileged (root-level) access to a computer while hiding its presence.
Botnet: A network of infected computers (zombies) controlled by a central server (C&C).
Fileless Malware: Exists only in RAM or uses legitimate system tools (PowerShell) to avoid detection by disk-based antivirus.


1.2 Malware Types by OS
Different operating systems have different architectures, so malware is often OS-specific.
1.2.1 Windows Malware
The most targeted OS due to its market share.

Examples: WannaCry (Ransomware), Zeus (Banking Trojan), Emotet.
Characteristics: Often targets .exe, .dll, registry keys, and PowerShell.

1.2.2 Linux Malware
Common in servers and IoT devices.

Examples: Mirai (IoT Botnet), XorDDoS.
Characteristics: Often targets web servers, SSH brute forcing, and IoT vulnerabilities. ELF binaries are common.

1.2.3 Mac Malware
Increasingly common as Mac adoption grows.

Examples: KeRanger (Ransomware), Shylayer (Adware).
Characteristics: Exploits .dmg files or specific macOS vulnerabilities.

1.2.4 Android Malware
Targets mobile devices.

Examples: Joker (Fleeceware), CovidLock (Ransomware).
Characteristics: Malicious APKs, often disguised as legitimate apps on third-party stores.


1.3 Malware Analysis
Definition: The art of dissecting malware to understand how it works, how to identify it, and how to defeat or eliminate it.
1.3.1 Need for Analysis

Incident Response: To understand the scope of a breach.
Signature Generation: To create antivirus signatures to detect the malware.
Attribution: To figure out who created the malware.
Remediation: To learn how to clean the infection.

1.3.2 Types of Analysis

Static Analysis: Analyzing the code or structure of the malware without running it.

Techniques: Hashing (MD5/SHA256), Strings analysis, PE Header analysis, Disassembly.
Pros: Safe, fast. Cons: Can be defeated by packing/obfuscation.


Dynamic Analysis: Running the malware in a controlled environment (Sandbox/VM) to observe its behavior.

Techniques: Monitoring API calls, network traffic, file system changes, registry changes.
Pros: Shows actual behavior. Cons: Malware can detect sandboxes and hide.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.filePath: Final Year Notes/Sem 6/Malware Analysis/Notes/Chapter 2 - Static Analysis.md
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.title: Chapter 2 - Static Analysis
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.content:
Chapter 2: Static Analysis
Subject: Malware Analysis (CDS-367A)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: static-analysis pe-file hashing strings obfuscation packing

2.1 Static Analysis Definition
Static Analysis involves examining the malware’s file structure and code without executing it.

Goal: To determine the file type, potential capabilities, and malicious intent safely.
Safety: Since the code isn’t run, there is no risk of infection during this phase (unless the analysis tool has a vulnerability).


2.2 Techniques of Static Analysis
2.2.1 Determining File Type (Fingerprinting)
Malware often misleads users by using fake extensions (e.g., invoice.pdf.exe).

Magic Numbers: The first few bytes of a file identify its true format.

MZ (4D 5A) = Windows Executable (PE).
%PDF = PDF file.
PK = Zip archive (or Office doc).


Tools: file command (Linux), Detect It Easy (DIE), PEiD.

2.2.2 Hashing (Fingerprinting the Malware)
A hash is a unique digital fingerprint of a file.

Algorithms: MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256.
Usage:

Generate the hash of the suspicious file.
Search for it on VirusTotal or MalwareBazaar.
If found, you can see previous analysis results (Signature verification).


Fuzzy Hashing (SSDeep): Used to detect similar malware files (variants) even if the hash is different.

2.2.3 Extracting Strings
Extracting readable ASCII and Unicode strings from the binary.

What to look for:

URLs/IP addresses (C2 servers).
File paths (e.g., C:\Windows\System32\evil.dll).
Registry keys.
Error messages (can reveal original source code paths).


Tool: strings command, Floss (can extract obfuscated strings).

2.2.4 Determining File Obfuscation & Packing

Obfuscation: Techniques to make code unreadable (e.g., dead code, instruction substitution).
Packing: Compressing or encrypting the executable to hide the code from static analysis.

Indicators:

High Entropy (randomness) in sections.
Few readable strings.
Small Import Address Table (IAT) with only LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress.




Tools: PEiD, Exeinfo PE (detects packer used, e.g., UPX).

2.2.5 Inspecting PE Header Information
The Portable Executable (PE) header tells Windows how to load the program.

Sections:

.text / .code: Contains the CPU instructions (executable code).
.data: Global/Static variables.
.rdata: Read-only data (constants).
.rsrc: Resources (Icons, Dialogs, Manifests).


Timestamp: Compilation time (can be faked, but often useful).
Import Table (IAT): Lists the DLLs and functions the malware uses.

Suspicious: URLDownloadToFile (Downloader), CryptEncrypt (Ransomware), SetWindowsHookEx (Keylogger).

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.filePath: Final Year Notes/Sem 6/Malware Analysis/Notes/Chapter 3 - Dynamic Analysis.md
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.title: Chapter 3 - Dynamic Analysis
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.content:
Chapter 3: Dynamic Analysis
Subject: Malware Analysis (CDS-367A)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: dynamic-analysis monitoring tools procmon wireshark dll

3.1 Dynamic Analysis Definition
Dynamic Analysis involves running the malware in a controlled environment (Sandbox or VM) to observe its behavior.

Safety: Must be done in an isolated network (Host-Only or Custom) to prevent the malware from spreading or contacting real attackers.


3.2 System and Network Monitoring
3.2.1 Monitoring Tools (The Toolkit)

Process Monitor (ProcMon):

Function: Captures real-time file system, registry, and process/thread activity.
Usage: Filter by “Process Name is [malware.exe]“. Look for CreateFile (dropping payloads) or RegSetValue (persistence).


Process Explorer (ProcExp):

Function: A supercharged Task Manager. Shows which handles and DLLs processes have opened.
Usage: Look for unusual child processes (e.g., svchost.exe spawned by malware.exe) or verify digital signatures.


RegShot:

Function: Takes a “Before” and “After” snapshot of the Registry to show exactly what changed.
Usage: Run 1st shot → Run Malware → Run 2nd shot → Compare.


Wireshark:

Function: Network packet sniffer.
Usage: Capture DNS queries (to find C2 domains) and HTTP requests (data exfiltration).


ApateDNS / INetSim:

Function: Fake DNS and Internet services.
Usage: Responds to all DNS queries with the analysis machine’s IP, tricking the malware into revealing its network behavior without connecting to the real internet.




3.3 Dynamic Analysis Steps

Baseline: Start the VM and run all monitoring tools (paused).
Snapshot: Take a VM snapshot (clean state).
Start Monitoring: specific filters in ProcMon/Wireshark.
Execute: Run the malware as Administrator.
Observe: Watch for 3-5 minutes (some malware sleeps to delay execution).
Stop & Analyze: Stop tools and look for “Badness” (new files, registry keys, connections).
Revert: Restore the clean VM snapshot.


3.4 DLL Analysis
Malware often uses DLLs (Dynamic Link Libraries) instead of EXEs to hide.

Execution: DLLs cannot run alone. They use rundll32.exe.

Command: rundll32.exe malicious.dll, ExportFunction


Analysis:

Use Dependency Walker to see exported functions.
Use ProcMon to watch rundll32.exe events.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.title: Chapter 4 - Assembly Language and Disassembly Primer
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.content:
Chapter 4: Assembly Language and Disassembly Primer
Subject: Malware Analysis (CDS-367A)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: assembly x86 registers stack instructions

4.1 Computer Basics
Malware analysis often requires reading Assembly Code because we rarely get the source code of malware. Assembly is the human-readable representation of Machine Code (1s and 0s).

4.2 CPU Registers (x86 - 32 bit)
Registers are small, super-fast storage locations inside the CPU.

General Purpose Registers:

EAX (Accumulator): Used for arithmetic and return values of functions.
EBX (Base): Base pointer for memory access.
ECX (Counter): Loop counter (used in REP instructions).
EDX (Data): I/O operations, extension for EAX in multiplication/division.
ESI (Source Index): Source pointer for string operations.
EDI (Destination Index): Destination pointer for string operations.


Pointers (Critical):

ESP (Stack Pointer): Points to the top of the stack. (Changes constantly).
EBP (Base Pointer): Points to the bottom of the current Stack Frame (Function). Used to access local variables and arguments.
EIP (Instruction Pointer): Points to the Next Instruction to be executed. If an attacker controls EIP, they control the CPU.


EFLAGS: Status flags (Zero Flag ZF, Sign Flag SF) used for conditional jumps.


4.3 Key Instructions
4.3.1 Data Transfer

MOV dst, src: Copies data from src to dst. (MOV EAX, 1 → Set EAX to 1).
LEA dst, [src]: Load Effective Address. Calculates an address (math) but doesn’t access memory. Often used for fast math.

4.3.2 Stack Operations

The Stack grows downwards (from High Memory to Low Memory).
PUSH src: Decrements ESP by 4, puts data at [ESP].
POP dst: Takes data from [ESP], puts it in dst, Increments ESP by 4.

4.3.3 Arithmetic & Logic

ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV.
XOR EAX, EAX: A fast way to set EAX to 0. (XORing something with itself always equals 0).

4.3.4 Control Flow

CMP A, B: Compares A and B by subtracting them and setting FLAGS.
JZ label: Jump if Zero (ZF=1). (i.e., Jump if A == B).
JNZ label: Jump if Not Zero (ZF=0).

4.3.5 Functions

CALL address:

PUSH next instruction address (Return Address) onto the stack.
JMP to the function address.


RET:

POP the Return Address from the stack into EIP.
(Execution resumes where called).




4.4 x64 Architecture

Registers are 64-bit: RAX, RBX, RIP, etc.
Calling Convention: First 4 arguments are passed in registers (RCX, RDX, R8, R9) instead of pure stack usage (Fastcall).

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.title: Chapter 5 - Disassembly Using IDA
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.content:
Chapter 5: Disassembly Using IDA
Subject: Malware Analysis (CDS-367A)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: ida-pro disassembly reverse-engineering flirt patching

5.1 Introduction to IDA Pro
IDA (Interactive DisAssembler) is the industry standard for Reverse Engineering and Static Analysis.

Function: It takes a binary (.exe) and recursively disassembles it into Assembly language instructions, while adding helpful comments and names.


5.2 Key Features for Analysis
5.2.1 Graph View vs. Text View

Graph View: Visualizes the Control Flow of a function using blocks and arrows.

Green Arrow: Jump taken (Yes/True).
Red Arrow: Jump not taken (No/False).
Blue Arrow: Unconditional Link.


Text View: Linear list of instructions (like reading a book). Good for details.

5.2.2 Cross-References (X-Refs)
IDA tracks where every function and data item is used.

Usage: If you find an interesting string (e.g., “Password Accepted”), you can use X-Refs (Keys: X) to find the CODE that references that string. This leads you directly to the password validation logic.

5.2.3 FLIRT Signatures
Fast Library Identification and Recognition Technology.

Problem: Binaries contain standard library functions (like printf, memcpy) mixed with malware code. Analysis is hard if everything looks the same.
Solution: FLIRT identifies these standard functions and renames them automatically, allowing the analyst to ignore them and focus on the custom malware logic.


5.3 Patching Binaries
IDA allows you to modify the instructions of a binary.

Use Case: Bypassing a security check (e.g., “Is Debugger Present?”).
Technique:

Locate the conditional jump (JZ exit_malware).
Patch it to NOP (No Operation) or force the jump (JMP).
Export the modified binary.




5.4 Scripting and Plugins
IDA is highly extensible using IDAPython.

Automation: You can write Python scripts to:

Decrypt strings automatically (e.g., if the malware uses XOR encoding).
Rename functions in bulk.
Identify crypto constants.


Plugins: Popular plugins include Keypatch (for easier patching) and ClassInformer (for C++ RTTI).

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.title: Chapter 6 - Debugging malicious binaries
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.content:
Chapter 6: Debugging Malicious Binaries
Subject: Malware Analysis (CDS-367A)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: debugging x64dbg ida-debugger breakpoints anti-debugging

6.1 General Debugging Concepts
Debugging allows you to pause malware execution, inspect memory/registers, and execute instructions one by one.
6.1.1 Breakpoints
A “Stop Sign” for the CPU.

Software Breakpoint (INT 3):

The debugger replaces the first byte of an instruction with 0xCC (INT 3).
Usage: Good for almost anything. Detection: Malware can scan its own code for 0xCC.


Hardware Breakpoint:

Uses special CPU debug registers (DR0-DR3).
Usage: Monitoring memory access (e.g., “Break when this variable is written to”). Harder for malware to detect.



6.1.2 Stepping

Step Into (F7): Execute the next line. If it’s a function CALL, go inside the function.
Step Over (F8): Execute the next line. If it’s a function CALL, run the whole function and pause after it returns.


6.2 Debugging with x64dbg
x64dbg (and x32dbg) is a modern, open-source debugger for Windows.

Key Features:

Scylla: Integrated tool to Dump a running process from memory to disk and Fix Imports. Used to unpack malware.
ScyllaHide: A plugin to hide the debugger from the malware (Anti-Anti-Debugging).
Patching: easy to assemble new instructions (Spacebar) and save the patch.




6.3 Debugging with IDA Pro
IDA has a built-in debugger that integrates with the disassembly view.

Local Debugging: Debugging a program on the same machine.
Remote Debugging: Debugging a program running on a different machine (e.g., Linux malware in a VM).

How: Copy linux_server (from IDA folder) to the Linux VM, run it, and connect IDA to the VM’s IP.




6.4 Debugging Scripts (Python)
Both IDA and x64dbg support Python automation.

Use Cases:

Unpacking: Run execution until a specific memory region is unpacked, then dump it.
De-obfuscation: Automatically step through code and log values to find the decrypted configuration.
