Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.title: Chapter 7 - Malware Functionalities and Persistence
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Malware-Analysis/.content:
Chapter 7: Malware Functionalities and Persistence
Subject: Malware Analysis (CDS-367A)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: persistence registry scheduled-task dll-hijacking c2 powershell

7.1 Malware Functionalities
Besides the payload (e.g., encrypting files), malware needs helper functions.

Downloader: Small code that downloads the actual large malware from the internet.
Dropper: A carrier file that contains the malware (compressed/encrypted) and “drops” it onto the disk.
Command & Control (C2): Communicating with the attacker’s server to receive commands (e.g., “Attack IP X”) or exfiltrate data.
PowerShell Execution: Using powershell.exe -w hidden -enc <base64> to run malicious scripts purely in memory (Fileless).


7.2 Persistence Mechanisms
Persistence ensures the malware runs automatically after a reboot.
7.2.1 Registry Run Keys (Most Common)
Malware adds an entry to these keys to start with Windows.

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run (Current User)
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run (All Users - Requires Admin)

7.2.2 Scheduled Tasks
Using Windows Scheduler to run the malware at specific times or events (e.g., “At Logon”).

Command: schtasks /create /tn "Updater" /tr "C:\malware.exe" /sc onlogon

7.2.3 Startup Folder
Putting a shortcut (LNK) or the EXE itself in:

%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup

7.2.4 Winlogon Registry Entries
Hooking into the Windows Logon process.

Userinit Key: HKLM\...\Winlogon\Userinit. Normally userinit.exe. Malware appends , C:\malware.exe.
Shell Key: Normally explorer.exe.

7.2.5 Image File Execution Options (IFEO)
A debugging feature.

Trick: Create a key for taskmgr.exe and set “Debugger” = malware.exe.
Result: Every time the user opens Task Manager, Malware runs instead (or alongside).

7.2.6 Accessibility (Sticky Keys)

Technique: Replace C:\Windows\System32\sethc.exe (Sticky Keys) with cmd.exe.
Result: Press SHIFT 5 times at the RDP login screen → System Level CMD (Backdoor).

7.2.7 DLL Search Order Hijacking

Mechanism: When an app loads a DLL (e.g., version.dll), it looks in the Current Directory first.
Attack: Place a malicious version.dll in the same folder as a legitimate app (e.g., Chrome). Chrome will load the malware DLL thinking it’s the system one.

7.2.8 COM Hijacking
Modifying the Registry (CLSID) to point a Component Object Model (COM) interface to a malicious DLL. Used by legitimate apps (like Explorer) to load malware silently.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Web
Subject: Web Science (CDS-363)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: web-history web1 web2 web3 tim-berners-lee

1.1 History of Web
The World Wide Web (WWW) was invented by Sir Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 at CERN. His goal was to allow scientists to share information easily. The first website went live in 1991.

1.2 Evaluation of Web Versions
The web has evolved through three major phases:
Web 1.0 (The Read-Only Web) - 1990-2004

Characteristics: Static pages, text-heavy, no user interaction.
Role: Users could only read content provided by the site owner.
Tech: HTML, Simple hyperlinks.

Web 2.0 (The Social Web) - 2004-Present

Characteristics: Dynamic content, User-Generated Content (UGC), Social Media.
Role: Users can read and write (e.g., posting on Facebook, uploading to YouTube).
Tech: AJAX, JavaScript, CSS3, Mobile Apps.

Web 3.0 (The Semantic/Decentralized Web) - Future

Characteristics: Intelligent, decentralized, machine-readable data.
Role: Users own their data (Read-Write-Own).
Tech: AI, Blockchain, Semantic Web (RDF).


1.3 Building Blocks of Web
The web stands on three pillars:

HTML (HyperText Markup Language): The structure of the page.
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol): The rule for transferring data.
URL (Uniform Resource Locator): The address of the resource.


1.4 Uniform Resource Locator (URL)
A standard way to locate a resource on the internet.
Structure: protocol://hostname:port/path?query

https: Protocol
www.google.com: Hostname (Domain)
/search: Path
?q=web: Query String

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.filePath: Final Year Notes/Sem 6/Web Science/Notes/Chapter 2 - Web Architecture.md
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.title: Chapter 2 - Web Architecture
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.content:
Chapter 2: Web Architecture
Subject: Web Science (CDS-363)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: web-architecture http browser server

2.1 Web Browser (The Client)
Software used to access the web (e.g., Chrome, Firefox).

Functions:

DNS Resolution: Converts domain name (google.com) to IP address.
Rendering: parsing HTML/CSS to display the page.
Requesting: Sending HTTP requests to the server.




2.2 Web Server
A computer (or software) that stores web site files and serves them to the client.

Examples: Apache, Nginx, IIS.
Role: Listens on port 80 (HTTP) or 443 (HTTPS) and responds to requests.


2.3 HTTP Protocol
HyperText Transfer Protocol is the foundation of data communication on the web. It is a Stateless protocol (it forgets everything after the transaction).
2.3.1 HTTP Methods (Verbs)

GET: Retrieve data (View a page).
POST: Send data (Submit a login form).
PUT: Update data (Replace a file).
DELETE: Remove data.

2.3.2 HTTP Status Codes

200 OK: Success.
301 Moved Permanently: Redirection.
400 Bad Request: Client error.
404 Not Found: Resource doesn’t exist.
500 Internal Server Error: Server crashed.

2.3.3 Two-Tier vs Three-Tier Architecture

2-Tier: Client ←> Database (Old school).
3-Tier: Client ←> Web Server (Logic) ←> Database (Data). Used in almost all modern web apps.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.filePath: Final Year Notes/Sem 6/Web Science/Notes/Chapter 3 - Approaches to Web App Development.md
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.title: Chapter 3 - Approaches to Web App Development
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.content:
Chapter 3: Approaches to Web Application Development
Subject: Web Science (CDS-363)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: web-development templates programmatic approaches

3.1 Programmatic Approach
Writing code from scratch (or using frameworks) to generate HTML dynamically.

How it works: Code (PHP/Python/Node.js) queries a database and loops through results to print HTML tags.
Pros: Complete control, high performance, custom features.
Cons: Slower development time, requires skilled developers.
Example: Using Python Django or Raw PHP to build a custom dashboard.


3.2 Template Approach
Using pre-built static layouts with “holes” for data.

How it works: A designer creates an HTML file with placeholders like {{ username }}. The engine fills these spots.
Pros: Separation of concerns (Designers touch HTML, Developers touch Code), Faster development.
Examples: WordPress Themes, Jinja2 (Python), Blade (Laravel).


3.3 Hybrid Approach
Combining both methods. Using a template engine that allows some logic (Loops/If statements) inside the HTML.

Pros: Best of both worlds.
Modern Web Apps: Most modern frameworks (React, Angular, Vue) use a component-based hybrid approach where Logic and View are tightly coupled but reusable.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.title: Chapter 4 - HTML and XML
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.content:
Chapter 4: HTML and XML
Subject: Web Science (CDS-363)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: HTML XML forms parsers DOM SAX

4.1 HTML (HyperText Markup Language)
The standard markup language for creating web pages.

Role: Defines the structure of the content (Headings, Paragraphs, Images).
Forms: Crucial for user input.

<form action="/login" method="POST">: The container.
<input type="text">: Text field.
<input type="submit">: Button.




4.2 XML (eXtensible Markup Language)
Designed to store and transport data, not to display it.

Difference from HTML:

HTML: Pre-defined tags (<h1>, <div>). Focus on Looks.
XML: Custom tags (<book>, <price>). Focus on Meaning.
Strictness: XML is case-sensitive and must be properly closed.



4.2.1 XML Document Structure
Must have a root element and be well-formed.
<library>
    <book id="1">
        <title>Harry Potter</title>
        <author>J.K. Rowling</author>
    </book>
</library>

4.3 XML Parsers
Software used to read specific data from an XML file.
4.3.1 DOM Parser (Document Object Model)

Method: Loads the entire XML file into RAM as a tree structure.
Pros: Can read and write (modify) the XML. Easy to navigate (Parent/Child).
Cons: High memory usage. Bad for huge files.

4.3.2 SAX Parser (Simple API for XML)

Method: Reads the file line-by-line (Stream based). Triggers events when it sees a tag (e.g., startElement, endElement).
Pros: Fast, Low memory usage. Good for huge files.
Cons: Read-only (cannot modify the file). Can’t look backward in the file.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.filePath: Final Year Notes/Sem 6/Web Science/Notes/Chapter 5 - Security Development Lifecycle.md
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.title: Chapter 5 - Security Development Lifecycle
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.content:
Chapter 5: Security Development Lifecycle (SDL)
Subject: Web Science (CDS-363)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: SDL agile security threat-modeling

5.1 Introduction to SDL
Traditionally, security was an afterthought (“We’ll fix it after release”). SDL integrates security into every phase of the SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle).

Goal: To reduce the number and severity of vulnerabilities in software.


5.2 Agile SDL
Agile development is fast (Sprints). Traditional SDL is slow (heavy documentation). Merging them requires “Shift-Left Security”.

Core Practices:

Threat Modeling: Done every sprint for new features.
Automated Testing: Security scans (SAST/DAST) run automatically in the CI/CD pipeline.
Security Requirements: Treated as “User Stories” (e.g., “As a user, I want my password to be encrypted”).
Definition of Done (DoD): A feature isn’t “done” until it passes security checks.




5.3 Phases of SDL

Training: Developers learn secure coding.
Requirements: Define security gates (e.g., “All inputs must be sanitized”).
Design: Threat Modeling (What can go wrong?).
Implementation: Writing secure code, avoiding unsafe functions.
Verification: Fuzz testing, Penetration testing.
Release: Final security review.
Response: Incident response plan for when a hack happens.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.filePath: Final Year Notes/Sem 6/Web Science/Notes/Chapter 6 - Server-Side Web Security.md
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.title: Chapter 6 - Server-Side Web Security
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.content:
Chapter 6: Server-Side Web Security
Subject: Web Science (CDS-363)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: sqli injection server-security truncation

6.1 SQL Injection (SQLi)
The most dangerous web vulnerability. It occurs when untrusted user input is directly concatenated into a database query.

Mechanism:

Query: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '$user_input';
Input: ' OR '1'='1
Result: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'; (Returns ALL users).



6.1.1 Types of SQLi

In-band (Classic): The attacker sees the results (e.g., error messages or data dump) on the page.
Inferential (Blind): No data is returned, but the page behaves differently (e.g., loads slower) based on True/False queries.
Out-of-band: The database makes a DNS/HTTP request to the attacker’s server.


6.2 Stored Procedure Attack
Stored Procedures are often safe, unless they use Dynamic SQL (building a query string inside the procedure).

Risk: If variables are not parameterized inside the procedure, injection is still possible.


6.3 SQL Column Truncation
A logical flaw where the database cuts off input that is too long.

Attack Scenario:

Database stores username as VARCHAR(5).
Attacker registers as admin       x.
Database truncates it to admin (the spaces and ‘x’ are removed).
Attacker now has an account named admin with a password they chose, potentially overwriting or impersonating the real admin.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.title: Chapter 7 - Authorization and Authentication
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.content:
Chapter 7: Authorization and Authentication
Subject: Web Science (CDS-363)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: access-control authentication privilege-escalation horizontal-escalation vertical-escalation

7.1 Authentication vs. Authorization

Authentication (Who are you?): Verifying the identity of a user (e.g., Login with Username/Password, TFA).
Authorization (What can you do?): Verifying if the authenticated user has permission to access a specific resource (e.g., Admin vs. User permissions).


7.2 Access Control Models

Vertical Access Control (Role-Based):

Restricts access based on user hierarchy (e.g., Admin > Manager > Employee).
Vulnerability: Vertical Privilege Escalation occurs when a lower-privileged user accesses higher-privileged functions (e.g., a standard user accessing /admin/deleteUser).


Horizontal Access Control (Data-Based):

Restricts access to specific data sets for users with the same role (e.g., User A can see their own profile, but not User B’s profile, even though both are “Users”).
Vulnerability: Horizontal Privilege Escalation (IDOR - Insecure Direct Object Reference).

Example: Changing user_id=123 to user_id=124 in the URL to view another user’s data.






7.3 Privilege Escalation

Definition: An attack where an adversary gains elevated access to resources that are normally protected from an application or user.
Prevention:

Implement Principle of Least Privilege.
Use indirect references (Map IDs to random tokens) to prevent IDOR.
Enforce access control checks on every request, not just the front-end menu.

Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.title: Chapter 8 - Web Services
Final-Year-Notes/Sem-6/Web-Science/Notes.content:
Chapter 8: Web Services
Subject: Web Science (CDS-363)
Semester: Sem 6
Tags: soap wsdl uddi xml web-services

8.1 Introduction to Web Services
A Web Service is a standardized way for two different applications to communicate with each other over the internet, regardless of the operating system or programming language they use (e.g., a Java app on Linux talking to a .NET app on Windows).

8.2 Component Architecture
The classic Web Services architecture (Big Web Services) relies on three XML-based standards:
8.2.1 SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol)

Function: The Communication Protocol. It defines the format of the message being sent.
Structure:

Envelope: Wraps the entire message.
Header: Optional meta-data (auth, routing).
Body: The actual message payload (request or response).


Pros: Language independent, platform independent, works over HTTP/SMTP.
Cons: Verbose (lots of XML tags), slower than REST.

8.2.2 WSDL (Web Services Description Language)

Function: The Manual/Contract. It describes what the web service does.
Content:

What functions are available? (e.g., getPrice, placeOrder)
What are the input parameters? (e.g., string itemID)
What is the return type? (e.g., double price)
Where is the service located? (URL)


Analogy: WSDL is like the menu in a restaurant; it tells you what you can order.

8.2.3 UDDI (Universal Description, Discovery, and Integration)

Function: The Phonebook/Directory. It allows businesses to list their web services so others can find them.
Current Status: Largely obsolete in the public web; mostly used within large internal enterprise networks now.


8.3 REST vs. SOAP

REST (Representational State Transfer):

Paper-light, uses standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).
Typically uses JSON (easier to read/parse).
State of the art for modern web apps.


SOAP:

Rigid standard, high security (WS-Security).
Uses XML.
Common in legacy enterprise and banking systems.
